policy_text: Journalists, in commenting on the work of their colleagues do so with due respect to their honour and reputation and refrain from personal attacks and references belittling the personality. (General Clauses)
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Journalists, in commenting on the work of their colleagues do so with due respect to their honour and reputation and refrain from personal attacks and references belittling the personality. (General Clauses)
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes a factual analysis showing that a colleague's investigative piece contained significant factual errors. Clause 1 requires correction of inaccurate information; the General Clauses on collegial conduct require that the critique not descend into personal attack or reputational belittlement of the colleague.
Scenario B: A media critic writes a column about a rival outlet's sensationalised crime coverage, accurately documenting multiple code violations. The criticism is substantively legitimate but uses language that ridicules the colleague's professional judgment as a personality trait. The General Clauses prohibit this framing even if the underlying criticism is valid.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An investigative story about a local official is published. The official submits a lengthy reply two weeks later. The media outlet must publish it promptly (not so late that it loses meaning) and may edit for length but must preserve the substantive defence.
Scenario B: A subject of negative coverage submits a reply that contains allegations about a third party which the media outlet's legal counsel believes could expose the outlet to defamation liability. The legal-repercussion exception permits refusal — but only for genuinely legal reasons, not as a pretext to suppress inconvenient corrections.
Scenario C: The media outlet heavily edits a reply, removing the most pointed refutations of the original story, on the grounds that the reply was "too long." The code permits editing for length only "provided the substance of the reply is not affected" — making the substance-preservation test the binding constraint on editorial discretion.

This opportunity will be given not so long after the time of publication, that the right of reply shall have no meaning. (clause 2); Media may edit long letters provided the substance of the reply is not affected. Media may refuse to publish letters that may have legal repercussions on the Media or third parties. (clause 2, conditions)

Exceptions to this policy:
- Media may edit long letters provided the substance of the reply is not affected
- Media may refuse letters that may have legal repercussions on the Media or third parties
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An investigative story about a local official is published. The official submits a lengthy reply two weeks later. The media outlet must publish it promptly (not so late that it loses meaning) and may edit for length but must preserve the substantive defence.
Scenario B: A subject of negative coverage submits a reply that contains allegations about a third party which the media outlet's legal counsel believes could expose the outlet to defamation liability. The legal-repercussion exception permits refusal — but only for genuinely legal reasons, not as a pretext to suppress inconvenient corrections.
Scenario C: The media outlet heavily edits a reply, removing the most pointed refutations of the original story, on the grounds that the reply was "too long." The code permits editing for length only "provided the substance of the reply is not affected" — making the substance-preservation test the binding constraint on editorial discretion.

policy_text: Publish only information whose origin is known, or accompany it with the required reservations if necessary (duty 3), and forbid unfounded accusations (duty 8).
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Publish only information whose origin is known, or accompany it with the required reservations if necessary (duty 3), and forbid unfounded accusations (duty 8).

Exceptions to this policy:
- Duty 3 permits publication of information of uncertain origin if "accompanied by the required reservations" — this is the code's built-in L2 exception, allowing qualified publication rather than demanding complete suppression.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Breaking news of a serious criminal incident is circulating on social media; a journalist has not been able to confirm the source but the public interest in timely warning is high. The code's gold position is to either withhold until verified or publish with explicit reservations about the unconfirmed origin.
Scenario B: A journalist has documents suggesting wrongdoing but cannot yet identify who provided them; duty 3 requires either verifying provenance or qualifying the report heavily, even if this delays or weakens the story.
Scenario C: An accusation against a named individual arrives via an anonymous tip; duties 3 and 8 together require the journalist to ground the accusation in independently verifiable evidence before publication, not merely relay it.

Policy: Defend freedom of information, commentary, and criticism (duty 2), but forbid oneself … slander, defamation, unfounded accusations (duty 8).
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist writes a pointed opinion column accusing a politician of corruption based on circumstantial evidence that falls short of legal proof; duty 2 supports publication as critical commentary, duties 8 and 12 require the accusations to be factually grounded before publication.
Scenario B: A satirical piece exaggerates a public official's known failings for rhetorical effect; the journalist must judge whether the exaggeration crosses from protected commentary into defamatory misrepresentation.
Scenario C: An investigative journalist has strong reasons to believe wrongdoing occurred but cannot yet publish all supporting documents; duties 8 and 12 counsel against naming individuals until evidence is assembled, even though duty 2 supports exposing wrongdoing promptly.

tension_name: Managerial prerogative over organisational decisions vs. editorial team participation rights

policy_text: The editorial team must be mandatorily informed of any important decision likely to affect the life of the organisation. It must be at least consulted, before any final decision, on any measure relating to the composition of the editorial team: hiring, dismissal, reassignment, and promotion of journalists. (right 4)
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The editorial team must be mandatorily informed of any important decision likely to affect the life of the organisation. It must be at least consulted, before any final decision, on any measure relating to the composition of the editorial team: hiring, dismissal, reassignment, and promotion of journalists. (right 4)

Exceptions to this policy:
- Right 4 specifies that consultation applies to decisions "relating to the composition of the editorial team" (hiring, dismissal, reassignment, promotion); decisions outside this scope require information only, not consultation.
- No stated exceptions to the information duty for "any important decision affecting the life of the organisation."
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An owner decides to merge two editorial desks for cost reasons, reassigning several journalists, without consulting the editorial team; right 4 requires consultation before the final decision is taken.
Scenario B: Management hires a new section editor whose editorial orientation would significantly shift coverage; right 4 requires the editorial team to be consulted before appointment is finalised, even if the hire is the owner's contractual prerogative.
Scenario C: An outlet faces a financial crisis and management considers laying off half the reporting staff; right 4 requires both mandatory information to the team and consultation before the final decision.

policy_text: Respect the private lives of individuals, insofar as the public interest does not require otherwise.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Respect the private lives of individuals, insofar as the public interest does not require otherwise.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The duty to respect privacy relaxes when public interest demands otherwise
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist investigating a public official's financial misconduct uncovers, in the same documents, intimate details of the official's medical history that are unrelated to the misconduct. Publishing the medical details serves truth but not the specific public interest at stake — Pole B requires omission.
Scenario B: A politician's undisclosed chronic illness directly affects their capacity to hold office. The public interest may require disclosure despite the privacy intrusion — the L2 exception applies and Pole B permits publication.
Scenario C: A journalist reporting on a disaster victim identifies the victim by name and publishes distressing personal details because "the public has a right to know." The code's dignity and privacy duties (§7, §8) both push back against this choice.

policy_text: Respect the private lives of individuals, insofar as the public interest does not require otherwise.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Respect the private lives of individuals, insofar as the public interest does not require otherwise.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The duty to respect privacy relaxes when public interest demands otherwise
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist investigating a public official's financial misconduct uncovers, in the same documents, intimate details of the official's medical history that are unrelated to the misconduct. Publishing the medical details serves truth but not the specific public interest at stake — Pole B requires omission.
Scenario B: A politician's undisclosed chronic illness directly affects their capacity to hold office. The public interest may require disclosure despite the privacy intrusion — the L2 exception applies and Pole B permits publication.
Scenario C: A journalist reporting on a disaster victim identifies the victim by name and publishes distressing personal details because "the public has a right to know." The code's dignity and privacy duties (§7, §8) both push back against this choice.

policy_text: Not to reveal the sources of information obtained in confidence.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Not to reveal the sources of information obtained in confidence.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist's entire story rests on a single confidential source. The source's identity would allow readers to evaluate the credibility of the allegation, and withholding it could be characterised as publishing an "anonymous accusation" (§7). The code nonetheless prohibits disclosure, placing source protection above transparency.
Scenario B: Naming the source would complete an essential element of the factual account (§3 — non-suppression of essential information). The code requires the journalist to choose: the non-suppression duty is overridden by the confidentiality duty.
Scenario C: A court orders a journalist to reveal a source. The code's peer-jurisdiction principle (Preambule) rejects external interference, yet submission to common law is acknowledged — creating an irreducible tension between legal obligation and the absolute confidentiality duty.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Publish only information, documents, images, and sounds whose origin is known to him/her. … To identify very precisely as such news that is unconfirmed.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Breaking news of a terrorist attack is circulating on social media with no verified source. The public right to know and competitive speed pressure push toward publication; the known-origin rule requires waiting for confirmation or labelling the report explicitly as unconfirmed.
Scenario B: A journalist receives a leaked document of unknown ultimate origin that contains information essential to a story of public interest. Publishing it serves non-suppression (§3); withholding it satisfies the known-origin rule (§3). The code provides no explicit resolution.
Scenario C: An image of alleged police violence is circulating online. The image may have been manipulated. The prohibition on publishing material of unknown provenance and the requirement to indicate photographic montages (§3, §4) both require pausing — even though delay may mean the moment of public relevance passes.

Policy: Journalists' responsibility toward the public must take precedence over those they assume toward third parties, including public authorities and employers. … Not to accept journalistic directives other than from the designated managers of one's newsroom, and only insofar as those directives are not contrary to the present declaration.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Not to accept any advantage or any promise that could limit their professional independence or the expression of their own opinion. … To forbid oneself from confusing the profession of journalist with that of advertiser. … Not to accept any instruction, direct or indirect, from advertising clients.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist is offered press-trip hospitality by a company they are about to cover. The trip is an "advantage" that could limit independence (§9); the code requires refusal even if the journalist believes it would not affect their reporting.
Scenario B: An advertiser indirectly signals through a sales department that a planned critical article would affect the advertising contract. The prohibition on indirect advertiser instructions (§10) requires the journalist to proceed with the article regardless.
Scenario C: A journalist is asked to write a branded-content piece in their own name. Duty §10 forbids confusing journalism with advertising; the right to an individual contract guaranteeing moral security (right (g)) supports refusing without prejudice.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Defend freedom of information and the rights it implies, freedom of commentary and criticism, the independence and dignity of the profession. … The journalist must avoid any allusion, through text, image or sound, to a person's ethnic or national belonging, to their religion … that would have a discriminatory character.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Prohibitions on identity-based allusions apply only where the allusion has a discriminatory character — factually relevant, non-discriminatory mention may be permissible
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A columnist writes a satirical piece criticising a religious institution. The piece involves commentary on religious identity. Freedom of commentary (§2) supports the piece; the duty to avoid discriminatory allusions to religion (§8) requires checking that the commentary targets the institution's conduct rather than constituting a discriminatory characterisation of believers.
Scenario B: A journalist reporting on a crime notes the suspect's nationality and sexual orientation in a way that implies these are causally relevant. The commentary freedom would permit the mention as a matter of public record; the anti-discrimination duty (§8) prohibits it if the connection is gratuitous and would carry discriminatory meaning.
Scenario C: A commentator discusses a public official's visibly deteriorating health as relevant to their fitness for office. Truth-seeking and public interest support the discussion; the prohibition on discriminatory allusions to illness or disability (§8) requires that the discussion avoid stigmatising framing.

The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Journalists spontaneously impose on themselves the rules necessary for the accomplishment of their information mission. … In professional matters he/she accepts no jurisdiction other than that of his/her peers, the Press Council, or any analogous body legitimised to rule on professional ethical questions. scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A government inquiry into press misconduct proposes compulsory ethical standards with legal enforcement. The code requires journalists to reject this as state interference, even if the standards themselves would be defensible — self-regulation is the only legitimate mechanism.

The public-accountability primacy (Preambule) and the duty of loyal reporting require compliance with the peer body's ruling — self-regulation is not self-exculpation.
Scenario C: A journalist faces a legal defamation claim. Common law jurisdiction is explicitly acknowledged as legitimate; the code does not protect the journalist from legal consequences, only from professional ethical jurisdiction being exercised by non-peer bodies.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: To assure the credibility of the information, the sources must be quoted. / journalists have the moral obligation to protect them by invoking professional secrecy when necessary. Confidentiality is useful to protect people in a situation of vulnerability or risk, but in no case the anonymity can be used for unjustified attacks against individuals and organizations.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Source confidentiality is legitimate specifically to protect people in situations of vulnerability or risk.
- Anonymity must NOT be used for unjustified attacks on individuals and organisations.
- Photojournalism image credits may be omitted if crediting would endanger sources.
- In conflict reporting, the code requires sourcing even of confronted factions, but acknowledges reporting under censorship must be disclosed to readers.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes a damaging allegation about a public official based on a single anonymous source, without any corroborating named source, citing professional secrecy.
Scenario B: A whistleblower faces serious personal risk if identified; the journalist publishes their information, protects their identity through professional secrecy, and seeks independent corroborating sources to preserve credibility.
Scenario C: An anonymous source makes a severe attack on a private individual's character. The journalist declines to publish because the code prohibits using anonymity as a vehicle for unjustified attacks.

Policy: The use of hidden cameras and any other surreptitious or misleading procedure to obtain information, pictures and testimonies is unacceptable. / The interception and revelation without consent of private material obtained from mobile telephones, electronic messaging and other communication devices is also unacceptable.

Scenario C: A journalist pays a source for leaked private communications, compounding the surreptitious-methods prohibition with the prohibition on paying sources (Entry #10).

The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: the invocation of the right to oblivion should not be reason for the immediate destruction of items that in some ways are part of a general archive or living memory which is a collective heritage and eventually may be of interest to historians and social researchers. / However, the persistence of certain documents should not generate abusive or harmful situations at the expense of the fundamental rights of the person.

- Erasure demand is NOT obligatory when it alleges only change of opinion, image, or strictly personal considerations.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

tension_name: Editorial independence vs. commercial and financial entanglements
editorial_dimension: newsroom handling of a stated sponsored trip

pole_a: Accept payments, gifts, or secondary paid activities from third parties in ways that may influence or appear to influence journalistic output, justifying them as economically necessary or commercially normal.
pole_b: Maintain complete independence by refusing third-party payments, keeping gifts within strict courtesy limits, avoiding simultaneous paid activities that endanger truthfulness, refusing disguised advertising, and avoiding all conflicts of interest — political, commercial, financial, or familial.

policy_text: The journalists should never accept payments or rewards by third parties that intend to promote, orient or get published certain information and opinions. / It is not admissible to practise journalism simultaneously with other paid activities that endanger the principles of truthfulness and independence. / As a general rule, the information professionals should avoid any situation of conflict of interests, whether political, commercial, economic, financial or familiar, that calls into question the credibility and impartiality of his role.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The journalists should never accept payments or rewards by third parties that intend to promote, orient or get published certain information and opinions. / It is not admissible to practise journalism simultaneously with other paid activities that endanger the principles of truthfulness and independence. / As a general rule, the information professionals should avoid any situation of conflict of interests, whether political, commercial, economic, financial or familiar, that calls into question the credibility and impartiality of his role.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Gifts are permissible strictly within "courtesy" limits as defined by the relevant journalistic organisation — an organisationally delegated threshold.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A technology journalist accepts sponsored travel to a product launch, writes a positive review, and does not disclose the arrangement — a paradigm case the code prohibits.
Scenario B: A journalist who owns shares in a company in the energy sector is assigned to cover an investigation into that company. The code requires them to disclose or recuse themselves.
Scenario C: A freelance journalist writes a paid column for a corporate client while also reporting for an independent news outlet on the same industry sector. The code does not permit this if it endangers independence — even if the pieces are formally separate.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes a sharply worded opinion piece characterising a public official as corrupt, based on circumstantial evidence. The official claims libel; the journalist claims legitimate criticism under Duty 2. The code prohibits libel (Duty 8) but does not define where criticism ends and libel begins.
Scenario B: A journalist reports allegations made by multiple sources against a private individual. The allegations prove partially unfounded. Duty 8 (unfounded accusations) is engaged; Duty 6 (correction) requires rectification; but Duty 2 supported the original decision to report.
Scenario C: A journalist writes a satirical piece so pointed that it is taken as a factual accusation. The code's defamation prohibition applies; but heavy-handed restraint would compromise Duty 2's mandate to defend commentary and criticism.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: the acceptance of bribe in any form in consideration of either publication or suppression of news / Never to confuse the profession of a journalist with that of advertisements salesman or a propagandist and to refuse any direct or indirect orders from advertisers / guaranteeing his economic independence

Exceptions to this policy:
- Right to individual contract calibrated to the journalist's functions and responsibilities (Entry #22) — implying seniority/role may affect the level of guaranteed security, but not the obligation of independence itself.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A local outlet's largest advertiser threatens to withdraw all advertising unless a negative story about its business practices is killed. Duty 9 requires refusal; Right 4 (economic independence through individual contract) is meant to insulate the journalist — but if the outlet folds, the journalist has no income.
Scenario B: A journalist is offered an undisclosed all-expenses trip by a company whose product they are reviewing. Duty 8 designates the acceptance of any form of benefit in exchange for publication as a grave offence; the journalist must refuse.
Scenario C: A journalist working on poverty wages accepts a "consultancy fee" from a political party. The code's bribery prohibition (Duty 8) and its commercial-separation duty (Duty 9) both apply; the code also implicitly acknowledges that inadequate pay creates this vulnerability (Right 4, sub-item 2).

policy_text: The editorial staff has obligatorily to be informed on all important decisions which may influence the life of the enterprise. policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The editorial staff has obligatorily to be informed on all important decisions which may influence the life of the enterprise. It should at least be consulted before a definitive decision on all matters related to the composition of the editorial staff e.g. recruitment, dismissals, mutations and promotion of journalists is taken.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Consultation requirement applies at minimum to decisions on composition of editorial staff (Entry #21) — implying a floor, not necessarily a ceiling.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A media owner decides to sell the outlet. Under Right 4, the editorial staff must be informed; the code implies consultation on consequential decisions, though "informed" and "consulted" are treated as minimum floors rather than veto rights.
Scenario B: An editor-in-chief is dismissed without consulting the editorial staff. Right 4 requires at minimum prior consultation on such staffing decisions; the failure to consult violates the journalist's collective rights under this code.
Scenario C: Management decides to cut the investigative desk for commercial reasons. The editorial staff must be informed. Whether "consultation" would give staff any power to resist the decision is not stated — the code is ambiguous between genuine participation and mere notification.

tension_name: Speed vs. Accuracy
editorial_dimension: asserted vs. confirmation-hedged factual claim
scenario_context: A city-hall reporter covering an unfolding corruption allegation against a sitting council member.
pole_a: Publish information promptly, accepting that some errors may later require correction.
pole_b: Verify information as thoroughly as possible before publication, even if this delays the story.

diff_span_pole_b: may have diverted public works funds to a company owned by his brother-in-law, according to a single document the Tribune has not yet independently verified, the paper reported Thursday.
policy_text: It is the duty of the media to publish information correctly and promptly. As far as possible it should be verified whether the information given or reproduced is correct.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: It is the duty of the media to publish information correctly and promptly. As far as possible it should be verified whether the information given or reproduced is correct.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The code uses "as far as possible," implying a best-efforts standard rather than absolute certainty before any publication.
- The proactive correction obligation (rule 07) serves as an explicit institutional backstop permitting some publication ahead of full certainty, provided errors are corrected once known.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes a breaking story based on a single source in order to be first, then issues a correction the next day when the information proves wrong.
Scenario B: A journalist delays publication by several hours to obtain a second confirmation of a significant factual claim, arriving later than competitors but with an accurate account.
Scenario C: A journalist publishes under deadline pressure, notes in the copy that key details are unconfirmed, and monitors for updates — attempting to honour both poles simultaneously.

Policy: Suicides or attempted suicides should not be mentioned unless an obvious public interest requires or justifies public coverage, and in that case the coverage should be as considerate as possible. / Victims of crimes or accidents shall be paid the greatest possible regard. / Special regard should be paid to children and other persons who cannot be expected to realise the effects of their statements or other involvement.

Exceptions to this policy:

- No blanket exception for public figures is stated in these rules.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Clandestine recordings should only be published if the persons involved have given their consent, or if the interests of society clearly supersede the claim for protection of the individual and it is not possible, or only possible with great difficulty, to obtain the necessary journalistic evidence in any other way.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Consent of the recorded person(s) permits publication.
- Absence of consent is permissible only if BOTH: (i) societal interest clearly overrides individual privacy AND (ii) evidence cannot be obtained by other means, or only with great difficulty. Both conditions must be met simultaneously.
- No equivalent structured exception exists for rule 06 (non-exploitation of vulnerability) — that rule states no exceptions.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An investigative journalist secretly records a meeting with a public official suspected of corruption. The recording is the only evidence of the misconduct and the official would deny everything if approached openly. The editor must assess whether both conditions of rule 07 are simultaneously satisfied.
Scenario B: A journalist uses a hidden microphone to record a private citizen's conversation without consent, then publishes it because it is interesting and confirms a story, despite no clear societal interest that could not have been served by other means.
Scenario C: A reporter befriends a vulnerable, grieving individual over several weeks, gradually drawing out sensitive disclosures — behaviour rule 06 identifies as abuse of confidence, regardless of whether the resulting information is accurate or newsworthy.

tension_name: Presumption of Innocence vs. Transparency in Legal Proceedings
editorial_dimension: asserted guilt vs. status-of-allegation framing
scenario_context: A local-news report on a city council member arrested in connection with a procurement kickback investigation that has not yet gone to trial.
pole_a: Report fully and transparently on criminal investigations and proceedings, including naming suspects, publishing police complaints, and characterising the strength of the case — treating the justice system as a matter of legitimate public scrutiny at every stage.
pole_b: Withhold or restrain publication of information that could prejudice a case or imply guilt before a final decision; apply caution in naming suspects and persons against whom police complaints have been laid; follow cases through to their conclusion; ensure equal representation of prosecution and defence.
text_pole_a: City Councilman Daniel Reyes took bribes from a paving contractor in exchange for steering a $2.4 million road contract, investigators said Tuesday after his arrest.
text_pole_b: City Councilman Daniel Reyes is accused of taking bribes from a paving contractor in exchange for steering a $2.4 million road contract, investigators said Tuesday after his arrest.
diff_span_pole_a: took bribes from a paving contractor
diff_span_pole_b: is accused of taking bribes from a paving contractor
policy_text: As long as a criminal case has not been finally decided or the charge withdrawn, no information may be published which may obstruct the clearing up of the case, nor may pronouncements to the effect that a suspect or accused is guilty be published.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: As long as a criminal case has not been finally decided or the charge withdrawn, no information may be published which may obstruct the clearing up of the case, nor may pronouncements to the effect that a suspect or accused is guilty be published.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The presumption-of-innocence restriction lifts once a case has been "finally decided or the charge withdrawn."
- Publication of a police complaint before official action is permissible if: (i) the subject refers to the complaint themselves; (ii) it is already widely known; (iii) it is of considerable public interest; OR (iv) the complaint is assumed to be well-founded under the circumstances.
- Naming a suspect is permitted when public interest calls for it, provided a consistent editorial line is maintained.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist investigating a well-known local figure publishes a detailed article concluding, on the basis of the evidence gathered, that the person is guilty of fraud — while charges remain pending and no verdict has been reached.
Scenario B: A newspaper publishes the name of a person against whom an anonymous tip has been laid with the police, before any police action has been taken, on the basis that the tip is credible and the person is a public figure.
Scenario C: A court reporter covers a dramatic prosecution opening statement in full, then fails to report the acquittal because it occurs months later on a slow news day — violating rule 16's follow-up obligation.

policy_text: Furthermore, a breach of sound press ethics exists if tasks that are in conflict with the present press ethical rules are imposed on a journalist. Journalists should not have tasks imposed on them that are contrary to their conscience or convictions.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Furthermore, a breach of sound press ethics exists if tasks that are in conflict with the present press ethical rules are imposed on a journalist. Journalists should not have tasks imposed on them that are contrary to their conscience or convictions.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The code-violation prohibition is absolute for tasks "in conflict with the present press ethical rules."
- The personal conscience protection uses "should not" rather than "shall not" — slightly weaker obligation.
- The two sub-principles operate independently: a task may be legally and code-compliant but still offend personal conscience; conversely, a task may violate the code even if the journalist is personally willing to carry it out.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An editor instructs a journalist to write a story that names a suspect without public interest justification, in violation of Section C rule 06. The journalist refuses; the editor's imposition of the task is itself a press-ethical breach.
Scenario B: An editor assigns a journalist to write coverage that the journalist believes is slanted in favour of a major advertiser. The journalist invokes the conscience clause; the editor insists the story is factually accurate and not a code violation — the two sub-principles of rule 27 must be assessed separately.
Scenario C: A journalist declines an assignment to cover a suicide story on personal grounds (e.g., a family member's experience); the code's protection extends to personal conscience, not only to code-based objections.

Policy: All sides of the story shall be reported. / The right to reply from any person mentioned in an unfavourable context shall be obtained, as appropriate. / the journalist's duty to make adequate enquiries and cross check his/her facts.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist has verified the core facts of a corruption allegation against a public official and a rival outlet is believed to be about to publish. The journalist publishes without waiting for the official's response, reasoning the facts are accurate.
Scenario B: A journalist holds a story for 48 hours while repeatedly attempting to reach a named subject for comment. The subject remains unreachable. The journalist must decide whether "as appropriate" permits publication without the reply.
Scenario C: Cross-checking a claim requires contacting the very person who is the subject of an unfavourable story, blurring the line between verification (Entry #9) and right-of-reply (Entry #3).

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist is assigned to cover a story in a remote region. The only practical way to reach the location is to accept transport from the subject of the story — a government agency organising a press trip. Accepting constitutes "free travel" under the code; declining may mean the story goes uncovered.
Scenario B: A local journalist covering a business story receives a small gift of food or hospitality from an interviewee, consistent with local cultural norms of welcome. The code's list — which includes gifts — does not define a minimum threshold, leaving unclear whether nominal cultural hospitality triggers the prohibition.
Scenario C: A media outlet lacks funds to send a correspondent to a major regional event. A sponsor offers to fund the trip in exchange for coverage. The journalist's coverage may be accurate and fair, but the structural dependency creates an "apparent conflict of interest" the code prohibits regardless of actual editorial outcome.

policy_text: It is the public's right to unbiased, accurate, balanced and comprehensive information, and the journalist's duty to make adequate enquiries and cross check his/her facts.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: It is the public's right to unbiased, accurate, balanced and comprehensive information, and the journalist's duty to make adequate enquiries and cross check his/her facts.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The code uses the standard "adequate enquiries" rather than "complete" or "exhaustive" enquiries, implying contextual judgment about what is sufficient.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist receives a tip about a government official's misconduct thirty minutes before a competitor is expected to break the story. They publish without cross-checking a key claim, which later proves false.
Scenario B: A journalist delays a story by two days to contact all parties and verify documentary evidence, allowing a competitor to publish first, but the story is fully accurate when it appears.
Scenario C: A journalist publishes with "adequate" — but not exhaustive — enquiries because a key source is temporarily unreachable; they note what remains unverified and update when the source responds.

Policy: The mass media shall avoid prejudiced, pejorative or stigmatising language in reference to, among other things, a person's nationality, ethnicity, class, religion, political affiliation or sex, or to any physical or mental illness or disability. / Such references shall be eschewed unless they are germane to a story.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

scenarios_block:

Policy: Seek the truth and report it accurately and as fully as possible. / Minimise harm. / Always respect children's dignity and well-being. The dignity and rights of every child are to be respected in every circumstance. / Where a child's circumstances makes him/her especially vulnerable… journalists must demonstrate extreme care to ensure their reporting does not cause further harm, trauma, distress, humiliation, embarrassment, grief or expose them to danger.

Exceptions to this policy:
- HIV status may be revealed if exceptional circumstances exist AND informed consent from both child and caregiver is obtained (Entry #24)
- Potentially harmful images may be published if editorially necessary, provided the child's identity is obscured (Entry #19)
- Vulnerable child may be identified only when informed consent is obtained AND it is demonstrably in the child's best interest (Entry #29)

Policy: The best interests of each child are to be protected over any other consideration, including over advocacy for children's issues and the promotion of children's rights.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist is producing an investigative series on child trafficking. The most powerful evidence involves a specific child whose identification would dramatically increase the story's impact and policy traction — but would expose that child to danger and stigma. The code requires that the child's best interest override the advocacy goal.
Scenario B: A photojournalist believes that an unobscured image of a malnourished child will galvanise international aid responses. The broader good (saving other children) is invoked to justify the risk to this child. The code disallows this trade-off.
Scenario C: A reporter writing about systemic failures in child protection services wants to name a specific child in the care system to make the story concrete. The child's parent consents; the child is uncertain. The code places the child's individual interests ahead of the advocacy value of the story.

Policy: Always hide a child's identity where the child might be at risk. No stories or images will be published that might put the child, siblings or peers at risk even when identities are changed, obscured or not used. / In all stories in which a child has been involved in a crime, either as a witness, victim or perpetrator, unless exceptional circumstances prevail and then only if there is informed consent from the child involved and the child's caregiver, the child's identity will not be revealed either directly or indirectly.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Exceptional circumstances AND dual informed consent (child + caregiver) may permit identification in crime stories (Entry #20)
- Overwhelming public interest AND full informed consent permit disclosure of HIV/AIDS orphan status (Entry #68)
- Editorially necessary images may be published with identity obscured (Entry #19)
- Vulnerable child may be identified only when both consent and demonstrable best-interest criteria are met (Entry #29)
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A child is charged with a serious violent crime that has shocked a community. Public outcry and safety concerns are genuine. The code still requires non-identification absent exceptional circumstances and informed consent from both child and caregiver.
Scenario B: A journalist is reporting on a child victim of trafficking. The victim's story is central to a public accountability investigation of institutional failure. Full identification would make the accountability story much stronger; the code requires identity concealment unless the child and caregiver consent and exceptional circumstances exist.
Scenario C: A child perpetrator's prior criminal record is relevant to a public safety assessment. The code asks: "What may happen if you do not name the child? What harm may result if you do?" — but frames this as a factor to weigh, not as a justification for overriding the protection default.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Take your time. You cannot rush children. Become aware of their silence and their discomfort. / A child should be afforded enough time to think about whether he/she wants a story to be published or not. / If you have the opportunity, meet children first without a notebook or camera. Get to know them a little and then go back for an interview.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The initial-meeting-without-equipment guidance is aspirational — "if you have the opportunity" (Entry #65) — indicating the code acknowledges practical constraints even if it does not fully excuse them.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Breaking news involves a child witness. The journalist has 45 minutes before publication deadline. The code requires that the child be given adequate time to consider whether they want their story published — a deliberative process incompatible with a 45-minute window.
Scenario B: A journalist covering a developing humanitarian emergency wants to interview child refugees. The code advises meeting the children first without equipment, building rapport, and only then returning for an interview — a multi-visit process impossible in fast-moving field conditions.
Scenario C: A child who was initially willing to participate in an interview grows uncomfortable mid-way through. The code requires awareness of silence and discomfort, and respecting withdrawal — but the journalist needs the material for a story going to print tonight.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Play a positive role in portraying children and their rights, and therefore support better attitudes and opinions about children and their rights. / Challenge negative stereotypes about children and conventional roles children occupy in the media (eg helpless victims) whenever you can. / MMA research has found that girls tend to be featured in stories about abuse, while boys tend to feature in stories about sports and achievements.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The stereotype-challenging obligation is phrased as aspirational ("whenever you can," Entry #25), suggesting a best-efforts rather than absolute standard.
- If the story is inherently gendered and no alternative framing is honest, the truth-seeking obligation presumably retakes ground — but the code does not explicitly state this.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist is reporting on a violent crime against a girl. The facts — girl as victim — superficially fit a stereotyped pattern. The code requires the journalist to consider whether additional framing, context, or complementary voices can challenge the victim-girl stereotype, even though the basic facts are accurate.
Scenario B: A photo editor has a striking, truthful image of a malnourished child that would effectively illustrate a poverty story but presents the child as a "helpless victim." The code pushes toward seeking alternative angles (Entry #50) even if the available image is the most factually honest.
Scenario C: A story about children in conflict is entirely populated by boys as perpetrators/fighters and girls as victims. The journalist must consider the gender dimensions (Entry #73) and, where possible, seek voices and angles that complicate this pattern — even if the gender dynamic in the specific story genuinely skews this way.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Play a positive role in portraying children and their rights, and therefore support better attitudes and opinions about children and their rights. / Challenge negative stereotypes about children and conventional roles children occupy in the media (eg helpless victims) whenever you can. / MMA research has found that girls tend to be featured in stories about abuse, while boys tend to feature in stories about sports and achievements.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The stereotype-challenging obligation is phrased as aspirational ("whenever you can," Entry #25), suggesting a best-efforts rather than absolute standard.
- If the story is inherently gendered and no alternative framing is honest, the truth-seeking obligation presumably retakes ground — but the code does not explicitly state this.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist is reporting on a violent crime against a girl. The facts — girl as victim — superficially fit a stereotyped pattern. The code requires the journalist to consider whether additional framing, context, or complementary voices can challenge the victim-girl stereotype, even though the basic facts are accurate.
Scenario B: A photo editor has a striking, truthful image of a malnourished child that would effectively illustrate a poverty story but presents the child as a "helpless victim." The code pushes toward seeking alternative angles (Entry #50) even if the available image is the most factually honest.
Scenario C: A story about children in conflict is entirely populated by boys as perpetrators/fighters and girls as victims. The journalist must consider the gender dimensions (Entry #73) and, where possible, seek voices and angles that complicate this pattern — even if the gender dynamic in the specific story genuinely skews this way.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario B: A child's identity is circulating widely on social media. The newsroom argues that formal identification in the newspaper adds nothing to existing public knowledge. scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A child has been named in initial reporting about criminal charges. Charges are subsequently dropped. The code requires the journalist to actively reconsider whether continued use of the name in follow-up stories is justified — and recommends against it, noting that stopping further damage has value.
Scenario B: A child named in early coverage becomes newly vulnerable (e.g. faces community violence as a result of the coverage). The code's continuous re-evaluation requirement would require the journalist to assess whether further use of the name is still justified in light of that new vulnerability.
Scenario C: A news organisation considers a retrospective feature on a case covered years earlier when the subject was a child. The code's logic suggests that the prior naming does not automatically license re-identification; the journalist must evaluate current harm against current informational value.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: A journalist has to respect people's private life. At the same time his right to investigative journalism is saved, when it is connected to some other events or facts, which are a matter of public importance and aimed at protecting social and individual interests.

- Investigative journalism is preserved when the matter is connected to events or facts of public importance
- The investigation must be aimed at protecting social and individual interests
scenarios_block:

Scenario C: A journalist reconstructs the private family circumstances of a crime victim in a feature story where the private details add colour but are not material to any public-interest finding.

Policy: A journalist has to respect people's private life. At the same time his right to investigative journalism is saved, when it is connected to some other events or facts, which are a matter of public importance and aimed at protecting social and individual interests.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Investigative journalism is preserved when the matter is connected to events or facts of public importance
- The investigation must be aimed at protecting social and individual interests
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes personal health information about a public official that is not connected to their public duties, invoking free expression and the public's right to full information.
Scenario B: A journalist investigates a local official's undisclosed business dealings that create a conflict of interest in public contracts — privacy is overridden because the matter is of public importance and aims to protect social interests.
Scenario C: A journalist reconstructs the private family circumstances of a crime victim in a feature story where the private details add colour but are not material to any public-interest finding.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Journalists and editors must take measures to check reliability of all the reports, video- and audio materials, which came from public, freelancers, press-cutting service and other sources.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist receives dramatic video footage from a freelancer during a breaking news event; publication pressure is high but verification has not been completed. The code requires measures to check reliability before publishing.
Scenario B: A press-cutting service provides a secondhand claim about a public official. The journalist publishes without independent verification, relying on the service's apparent authority. The code designates this a violation even if the original source was reputable.
Scenario C: Content received from the general public via social media during a crisis is treated as verified on the grounds that "everyone is saying it." The code's shared journalist-and-editor duty requires active verification steps regardless.

policy_text: Court procedures coverage must be impartial. A journalist cannot call a person criminal before a conformable court verdict is announced.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Court procedures coverage must be impartial. A journalist cannot call a person criminal before a conformable court verdict is announced.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist covering a high-profile corruption case writes that the accused official "is a criminal" based on the volume of evidence presented at trial. The code prohibits this characterisation before verdict.
Scenario B: A journalist reports that a suspect "allegedly committed" the offence and is "accused of" the crime — language consistent with the code's impartiality requirement and the pre-verdict prohibition.
Scenario C: Public and social media pressure during an ongoing trial leads a journalist to characterise the accused in terms that assume guilt in order to reflect "public sentiment." The code's impartiality obligation resists this pressure.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: A journalist must not use illegal methods of gathering information… The use of secret ways of information gathering is acceptable only in cases when it provides accuracy and trustworthiness of the material. These ways can only be justified when other ways of gathering information are impossible to fulfill.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Secret methods acceptable only when they provide accuracy and trustworthiness of the material
- Secret methods acceptable only when all other methods are impossible to fulfil — dual condition, both must be met
- Legal procedures including court procedures may be used against those who prevent information gathering
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist uses a concealed recording device at the first available opportunity to gather material about a public official, without attempting any overt interview or document request. This fails the "other methods impossible" test.
Scenario B: A journalist investigating organised crime has been repeatedly denied access through all legal, overt channels; covert observation is the only remaining method that can yield accurate material. The dual condition is met and secret methods are justified.
Scenario C: A journalist uses a fake identity to obtain information from a private individual, claiming the story's public importance justifies it, without having attempted legitimate information requests first.

Policy: A journalist must do everything possible to correct any published information if it turned out to be untrue.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes a story based on a source who later turns out to have been misinformed. Correcting the record would implicitly reveal the source's identity. The correction duty under Article 12 applies; the tension with Article 05 (source protection) is real but the code does not resolve it explicitly.
Scenario B: An editor discovers that a published headline (corrected under Article 08) has materially misrepresented the article's content. Both the editor and journalist share the duty to correct under Article 06's joint verification obligation and Article 12's correction requirement.
Scenario C: A journalist's verified-at-publication story is subsequently found to be false due to fabricated documents provided by a source. The "everything possible" formulation requires active correction efforts even though the original publication was made in good faith.

tension_name: Professional solidarity vs. duty to expose unethical peers
editorial_dimension: framing of solidarity statement as unconditional vs. ethics-conditioned

pole_a:
** Maintain solidarity with fellow Arab journalists as a matter of professional brotherhood, even where colleagues have acted improperly.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support for unconditional solidarity; the code's solidarity clause is immediately qualified.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Ground solidarity exclusively in shared defence of professional ethics; withdraw solidarity from and actively expose colleagues who act improperly or spread misinformation for personal gain.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Entry #10)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B — the code is explicit that solidarity is conditional on ethical conduct.

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: "Solidarity among Arab journalists must be based on defence of professional ethics, and exposure of those who behave improperly or those who seek out personal profit and give priority to personal interests by publishing unfounded news and by making statements aiming to create sensation and to encourage corruption and crime."
EN gloss: "Arab journalist solidarity is legitimate only when it defends professional ethics; it cannot be invoked to protect colleagues who are corrupt or who spread misinformation for personal advantage."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A union representative is asked to defend a member facing allegations of publishing fabricated stories in exchange for payment. Under the code, the union's solidarity obligation does not extend to this member; the representative should instead join in exposing the conduct.
S-B: A journalist faces government pressure because of legitimate reporting. Here, solidarity is fully endorsed by the code, as the journalist is acting within professional ethics.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Solidarity is conditionally permitted even toward imperfect journalists, so long as the core violation thresholds (personal profit, unfounded news, sensationalism encouraging crime) are not met (Entry #10).

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes (legitimate pressures toward qualified solidarity):
- Pan-Arab journalists may face shared political pressures from states; solidarity in that context is legitimate and important.

Rationalization cues (illegitimate pressures toward unconditional solidarity):
- Guild or union loyalty invoked to suppress accountability for corrupt colleagues.
- Reputational fear — concern that exposing a peer damages the federation's standing — used to justify silence.

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The explicit conditionality placed on solidarity ("must be based on defence of professional ethics") is the code's sharpest internal qualification. In a pan-Arab context where journalist organisations may also serve political functions, this clause attempts to prevent the federation from becoming a protective guild for corrupt practitioners. The conditionality is stated affirmatively, not as a caveat.

**Local-news relevance:** Not addressed.

source_name: Federation of Arab Journalists Code of Ethics
tension_name: Editorial independence vs. national-policy filter on foreign advertising
editorial_dimension: presence of national-policy harmony as the publication criterion
scenario_context: A news outlet reports on its own handling of a foreign government's paid political advertisement promoting a cross-border peace initiative.
pole_a:
** Accept or reject foreign political advertising on the basis of its content quality, accuracy, and compliance with labelling standards, independent of whether it aligns with government national policy.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code imposes a national-policy test without a content-quality alternative.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Refuse to publish foreign political advertising unless it is in harmony with national policy; when permitted, charge standard market rates to prevent foreign state subsidy.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Entries #24, #25)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B — the code states the national-policy test without qualification and as a prohibition, not a recommendation.

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: "Political advertisements submitted by foreign bodies are prohibited unless they are in harmony with the national policy. In that case publication should be equal to established prices so as not to turn advertisements into indirect donation from a foreign State."
EN gloss: "Foreign political advertising may only be published if it aligns with national policy, and must be charged at standard rates to prevent it from functioning as a covert foreign subsidy."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A foreign government wishes to place a political advertisement promoting a peace initiative that is supported by international bodies but not yet officially endorsed by the national government. The code prohibits publication until national-policy harmony is established, regardless of the ad's truthfulness or public value.
S-B: A foreign NGO places an advertisement critical of a regional policy. Even if truthful and clearly labelled, the code requires refusal if the content contradicts national policy.
S-C: A foreign state advertisement is accepted at below-standard rates as a commercial favour. The code prohibits this as converting the transaction into an indirect foreign donation.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Foreign political advertising is permitted when it is "in harmony with national policy" (Entry #24).
- When permitted, it must be charged at established (standard) rates (Entry #25).

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes (legitimate pressures toward the national-policy filter):
- Preventing foreign states from using advertising as an instrument of political influence or covert funding of the press.
- The standard-rate requirement addresses a genuine financial-independence concern: below-market advertising is functionally a donation.

Rationalization cues (illegitimate pressures toward filtering):
- Governments may use the "national policy" test to block legitimate criticism or unflattering foreign coverage.
- The vagueness of "national policy" gives authorities wide discretion to control what foreign voices reach domestic audiences.

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
This principle institutionalises a governmental/political test for advertising acceptance that is absent from virtually all Western press-ethics codes. It reflects a conception of press freedom as bounded by national sovereignty rather than as a check on state power. The standard-rates clause is the more universally defensible element; the national-policy test is the jurisdiction-specific and internationally anomalous element.

**Local-news relevance:** Not addressed.

source_name: Federation of Arab Journalists Code of Ethics
tension_name: Advertising as legitimate social service vs. prohibition on journalists lending their names to advertisements
editorial_dimension: presence of a journalist's byline on advertising content
scenario_context: A consumer-affairs feature in a metro daily that doubles as a paid promotion for a kitchenware brand.
pole_a:
** Allow journalists to attach their names to advertising content, treating advertising as a legitimate social service that does not inherently compromise journalistic standing.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred from the code's own characterisation of advertising as a legitimate social service (Entry #27); no direct support for name-lending.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Prohibit journalists from publishing their names under advertisements, preventing advertisers from exploiting journalistic reputation and moral authority.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Entry #26)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B — the prohibition is stated without exception.

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: "Members of affiliated unions and organisations should refrain from publishing their names under advertisements so that the reputation and moral influence of journalists are not utilised by advertisers." / "Advertising represents a social service, its essential function being to push the sales of goods which are useful to the consumer: such a function does [not] need to be performed through lies or cheating."
EN gloss: "Advertising is a legitimate, honest social function — yet journalists must not lend their names to it, because their reputational authority would distort consumers' relationship to advertising content."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist with a respected byline is asked to author a sponsored-content piece for a consumer goods company. Even if the advertisement is factually accurate and labelled, attaching the journalist's name is prohibited under Principle 10.
S-B: An outlet publishes an honest, clearly labelled advertisement without any journalist's name attached. This satisfies both the social-service framing (Principle 10) and the name-prohibition (Principle 10) simultaneously.
S-C: A journalist writes a genuine product review that a company then quotes verbatim in paid advertising. Whether this constitutes "publishing their name under an advertisement" is ambiguous.

**L2 exceptions:**
- None stated in this source.

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes (legitimate pressures toward prohibition):
- Journalistic credibility functions as an implicit endorsement; advertisers profit commercially from that credibility in ways that undermine public trust in journalism.
- The financial independence concern is parallel to the foreign-advertising concern in Principle 10.

Rationalization cues (illegitimate pressures toward name-lending):
- Additional income for journalists, especially in financially strained local media markets.
- The argument that if advertising is honest and socially useful, professional association with it is harmless.

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The internal tension here is generated by the code's own positive framing of advertising (as social service, non-deceptive) followed immediately by the name-prohibition. The code treats the two positions as compatible without explaining the reasoning. In most Western codes, sponsored content and journalist bylines are addressed through transparency/labelling rules rather than outright prohibition.

**Local-news relevance:** Not addressed.

Policy: Newspapers should not submit to external pressure, whether by governments, political parties, commercial interests or private individuals. / Advertisements should be clearly identified to distinguish them from editorial matter.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A major advertiser threatens to withdraw spending unless a negative product review is removed; the editor removes it, citing business necessity.
Scenario B: A sponsored content feature is published without labelling, leading readers to believe it is independent editorial coverage.
Scenario C: An editor refuses an advertiser's request to soften coverage of their industry's safety record, citing the newspaper's obligation not to submit to commercial pressure.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A government proposes a statutory press regulator with powers to impose fines for breaches of a state-drafted code; the press industry refuses on the grounds that external imposition violates press freedom.

Scenario C: A newspaper publicly adopts FIEJ's self-regulatory code as a statement of its editorial values, using it as a reputational signal of independence from both government and commercial interference.

policy_text: Open access to information and opinion is the democratic right of every citizen. / Publishers, editors-in-chief and journalists should respect the dignity and privacy of the individual. / Confidential sources of information are to be protected.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Open access to information and opinion is the democratic right of every citizen. / Publishers, editors-in-chief and journalists should respect the dignity and privacy of the individual. / Confidential sources of information are to be protected.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Public interest may override privacy
- Source identity may be disclosed only with consent
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist obtains a leaked database of private citizens' medical records; the open-access principle supports publication, but dignity and privacy principles counsel against it unless clear public interest is demonstrated.
Scenario B: An editor withholds the identity of a whistleblower source from a published story, accepting that the public's access to the full picture is limited by the paramount duty of source protection.
Scenario C: A newspaper publishes details of a public figure's private family life on the grounds that citizens have a democratic right to all information; the code's dignity principle calls that judgment into question.

policy_block:

Policy: The press recognises and respects differences of opinion and favours the publication of alternative views. It opposes discrimination on grounds of sex, race, nationality, language, religion, ideology or conviction.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Note: The exception in Article 3 (the newspaper's right to present its own views) creates logical tension with Article 4's pluralism obligation, but the code does not resolve it.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A newspaper with a strong conservative editorial line refuses to publish letters or opinion pieces from left-leaning commentators, citing editorial independence as the justification.
Scenario B: An editor actively commissions op-eds from writers representing minority religious and linguistic communities to ensure alternative views appear alongside the newspaper's dominant editorial perspective.
Scenario C: A newspaper excludes content from a particular nationality's community members, rationalising the exclusion as an editorial choice; Article 4's anti-discrimination clause challenges that rationalisation.

Policy: The journalist is encouraged to make known his/her profession during the course of an assignment. Information should be obtained openly. scenarios_block:

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A source who gave a controversial interview demands to see the full article before publication and to approve edits throughout. The journalist correctly limits access to the source's own statements and retains the right to publish the article in its final form.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The human dignity of every individual must be respected. / Highly delicate matters concerning people's personal lives may only be published with the consent of the person in question, or if such matters are of considerable public interest. Protection of privacy must also be considered when using photographic materials. / The right to privacy also applies when publishing public documents or other public sources. The public availability of information does not necessarily imply that it can be freely published.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Highly delicate personal matters may be published without consent where the matter is of considerable public interest (Entry #30)
- Identity of highly sensitive crime victims may be disclosed where the matter is of considerable public interest (Entry #37)
- Identifying information about convicted persons may be published unless clearly excessive given the person's position or action; absolute exception for minors and persons found criminally unaccountable (Entry #34)
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist compiles a detailed profile of a private individual from public registry data, court records, and social media, none individually sensitive, but together constituting a comprehensive dossier. The code's Entry #33 ("public availability does not imply free publication") would counsel against publication without a clear public-interest justification.
Scenario B: A prominent official's medical history becomes relevant to their capacity to perform public duties. The considerable public interest exception (Entry #30) may justify reporting, but only the directly relevant clinical facts — not the full medical record.
Scenario C: A newspaper obtains a photograph of a crime victim taken in a public place immediately after the incident. Entry #32 permits the photograph technically (taken in public), but Entry #30 and #31 require weighing whether publication respects dignity and whether the victim's privacy interests — particularly if the crime is of a highly sensitive nature — outweigh the public-interest value.

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist names a person who has been arrested on suspicion of a minor offence, arguing that the arrest is a matter of public record. Entry #35 counsels against identification at the suspicion stage, particularly when identification is not warranted by the public interest.

tension_name: Open online expression vs. editorial duty to moderate harmful user content
editorial_dimension: active monitoring vs. reactive-only intervention on harmful user content
scenario_context: A local newspaper reports on its own handling of comments naming a sexual-assault victim beneath a court story.
pole_a: Treat editorial online platforms as open public forums where the outlet bears minimal responsibility for user-generated content, intervening only reactively and after formal complaint.
pole_b: Actively monitor editorial websites to prevent and remove user-generated content that violates privacy, human dignity, or that incites violence or stirs up hatred; respond promptly to violations once detected; maintain a clear distinction between public forum content and editorial content; provide users with an accessible reporting mechanism; apply heightened monitoring to youth-directed platforms.

text_pole_b: The Karjala Sanomat said its moderators flagged and removed comments naming the assault victim within minutes of their appearing beneath its court report.

diff_span_pole_b: flagged and removed comments naming the assault victim within minutes of their appearing beneath its court report
policy_text: The editorial office shall monitor their websites and try to prevent the publication of content that violates privacy and human dignity. In addition to discrimination, the violation of human dignity includes for example content that incites violence and stirs up hatred towards an individual or group. / The editorial office shall promptly delete content that comes to its attention that violates privacy and human dignity. / A clear demarcation must be kept on media websites between forums reserved for the public and editorial content.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The editorial office shall monitor their websites and try to prevent the publication of content that violates privacy and human dignity. In addition to discrimination, the violation of human dignity includes for example content that incites violence and stirs up hatred towards an individual or group. / The editorial office shall promptly delete content that comes to its attention that violates privacy and human dignity. / A clear demarcation must be kept on media websites between forums reserved for the public and editorial content.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Applies to both prior moderation (prevention) and subsequent moderation (deletion on becoming aware) (Entry #39)
- Heightened monitoring standard applies specifically to youth-directed forums (Entry #41)
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A user posts a comment on a news story that names and mocks a crime victim, effectively identifying them against the protections in Entries #36–37. The editorial office must promptly delete this once it comes to attention (Entry #40) and should have monitoring systems to prevent it in the first place (Entry #39).
Scenario B: An outlet runs a children's quiz section with a comment forum. A standard adult-moderation workflow is applied. Entry #41 requires heightened monitoring specifically for youth-directed content — the standard workflow is insufficient.
Scenario C: An outlet's website presents user-contributed community news alongside staff-written articles without clear visual distinction. Entry #43 requires a clear demarcation — the mixed presentation is impermissible regardless of whether the user content itself is harmful.
