Policy: Editors' involvement must not alter the facts, context and attitudes of a journalist who signs the text/report. In case that the editor alters the facts, context and views expressed in the text/report, the journalist is obliged to clearly dissociate from these interferences. / If, by changing of the headline, title and subtitle, an editor changed the meaning and intonation of the text … a journalist is obliged to draw attention to the editor, and to require changes. If the editor does not accept requests from the journalist, they have the right to request the omission of signature, or to withdraw the texts.

Exceptions to this policy:
- If editorial changes alter facts, context, or views, the journalist is obliged to clearly dissociate.
- If the editor refuses corrections to a headline that changes meaning, the journalist may request omission of signature or withdraw the work.
- The editor is obliged to hear a journalist's request not to sign when signing would endanger the journalist's safety.
- A journalist may refuse to sign when changes are contrary to their opinion and belief, or when they have a reasonable personal security interest in not signing.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An editor rewrites a journalist's crime report to soften criticism of an advertiser. The journalist is obliged to dissociate from the altered version or request signature removal.
Scenario B: An editor changes a headline to be more sensational in a way that contradicts the article's conclusion. The journalist must alert the editor; if the editor refuses to correct it, the journalist may demand their name be removed.
Scenario C: A graphic editor alters the content of a photograph without the photographer's consent. This is impermissible; consent is required before any content change to an image.

In case that the editor alters the facts, context and views expressed in the text/report, the journalist is obliged to clearly dissociate from these interferences. / If, by changing of the headline, title and subtitle, an editor changed the meaning and intonation of the text … a journalist is obliged to draw attention to the editor, and to require changes. If the editor does not accept requests from the journalist, they have the right to request the omission of signature, or to withdraw the texts.

Exceptions to this policy:
- If editorial changes alter facts, context, or views, the journalist is obliged to clearly dissociate.
- If the editor refuses corrections to a headline that changes meaning, the journalist may request omission of signature or withdraw the work.
- The editor is obliged to hear a journalist's request not to sign when signing would endanger the journalist's safety.
- A journalist may refuse to sign when changes are contrary to their opinion and belief, or when they have a reasonable personal security interest in not signing.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: While collecting information, photos, documents, audio and video a journalist will only utilise honourable means. / Journalists and editors must not publish material acquired by using hidden cameras, listening devices, or unauthorised wiretapping, except when the public interest is protected (for example: disclosure of information regarding the threat to life and health of the population, corruption, abuse of power, etc.). / Concealing the identity of a journalist can be used only as the final means to obtain information: if other methods have been unsuccessfully applied, if the information cannot be obtained in any other way, and only when it relates to information of great importance to the public.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Covert surveillance material may be published when the public interest is protected — specifically: disclosure of threat to life and health, corruption, abuse of power. A clearly defined and transparent editorial procedure is required.
- Identity concealment may be used only as a final means, after other methods have failed, when information cannot be obtained otherwise, and only when of great public importance; the editorial board must be informed and legal advisors consulted.
- Questioning private individuals may continue after a request to stop only when there is a grounded public interest.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist uses a hidden camera to document a public official accepting a bribe in a setting where no other evidence is obtainable, other investigative methods have been exhausted, and the editorial board and legal advisors have been consulted. This falls within the narrow exception.
Scenario B: A journalist uses a false identity to infiltrate a corporate meeting to obtain a story that could be obtained through ordinary interview requests and document requests. This is impermissible; the "final means" requirement has not been met.
Scenario C: A journalist continues contacting a private individual after being asked to stop, justifying it as public interest reporting. The code permits this only when "grounded public interest" is at stake — the journalist must be able to demonstrate that public interest.

tension_name: Protecting Identity of Suspects/Victims vs. Public's Right to Know About Crime
editorial_dimension: named vs. anonymized identification of an unconvicted suspect
scenario_context: A local court reporter covering the arraignment of a man charged with embezzlement before any verdict has been reached.
pole_a: Full reporting on crime, including names, photos, and identifying details of suspects and victims, serves the public's right to know and enables public accountability for the justice system.
pole_b: Identity protection of suspects and victims — including withholding names, photos, addresses, appearance descriptions, marital and social status, and information about family and friends — is mandatory even when state authorities have already published the information.

diff_span_pole_a: Marko Petrović, 41, of Vračar,
diff_span_pole_b: A 41-year-old man
policy_text: The media are obliged to respect the right to the presumption of innocence and to protect the privacy and identity of the suspect or the perpetrator, even in the case of admission of guilt. / Even if the relevant state authorities publish information which are in the domain of privacy of the perpetrator or the victim, the media must not transmit that information.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The media are obliged to respect the right to the presumption of innocence and to protect the privacy and identity of the suspect or the perpetrator, even in the case of admission of guilt. / Even if the relevant state authorities publish information which are in the domain of privacy of the perpetrator or the victim, the media must not transmit that information.

Exceptions to this policy:
- These protections apply even after admission of guilt.
- State authority publication of identifying information does not grant media permission.
- Identity attributes may be mentioned only when directly related to the type and nature of the criminal offense.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Police publish the full name and photograph of a suspect before trial. The Serbian code prohibits republication; the state's disclosure does not create editorial permission.
Scenario B: A crime victim consents to be interviewed. The journalist may conduct the interview but still may not reveal the victim's or suspect's identity on the basis of that conversation.
Scenario C: A journalist reporting on a crime inadvertently reveals the suspect's identity by describing their physical appearance and neighbourhood. This indirect identification is prohibited.

Policy: A journalist does not report on issues in which they have private (personal or group) interest. / It will not be considered inappropriate if a journalist who has a personal interest reports on a subject if it is a matter of wider public interest (e.g., a journalist who lives in an area and writes about the need for a new school there).

Exceptions to this policy:
- Reporting despite personal interest is not inappropriate when the subject is of wider public interest — the code's own example: a journalist living in an area writing about local infrastructure needs.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist who lives in a neighbourhood writes about the need for improved public transport in that neighbourhood. Their personal stake is incidental and the subject is of wider public importance — the exception applies.
Scenario B: A journalist whose spouse works for a company writes a report assessing that company's business performance. The close relational interest and the commercial dimension both require recusal.
Scenario C: A journalist who owns shares in a company is assigned to report on that company's market performance. Recusal is mandatory.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: A journalist should not continue asking questions, phoning, photographing or recording a private person after they were asked to stop. / A journalist has the right, in relation to the state and other institutions, to continually ask questions that they believe are of public interest, regardless of whether they are asked to stop or not.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Pressure on a private person may continue after rejection only when there is a grounded public interest at stake.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A private individual involved in a story of minor public relevance asks a journalist to stop calling. The journalist must stop.
Scenario B: A government ministry refuses to respond to questions about a public health policy and instructs the journalist not to contact them further. The journalist has the right to continue.
Scenario C: A private individual is the only witness to a matter of great public safety importance and asks the journalist to stop. The code's "grounded public interest" override may apply, but the journalist must be able to demonstrate the grounding.

source_name: Slovakia Journalist's Code of Ethics (Slovak Syndicate of Journalists)
tension_name: Verification rigour vs. publication speed / agency reliance
editorial_dimension: number of independent sources cited
scenario_context: Political reporting on a cabinet reshuffle where the claim rests on sourcing breadth.
pole_a:
** Publish information verified by a single source, or rely on agency material without independent checking, in the interest of speed and efficiency.
**Pole A provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article III §4 exempts agency content from re-verification as the general rule)

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Verify every piece of information in at least two independent sources before publishing; re-verify agency material whenever doubt arises.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article III §1: "The information must be verified at least in two independent sources"; Article III §4 triggers re-verification on doubt)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Novinár je povinný overiť každú informáciu, ktorú publikuje. Informácia musí byť overená najmenej v dvoch nezávislých zdrojoch."*
EN gloss: "The journalist is obliged to verify every piece of information that he or she publishes. The information must be verified at least in two independent sources."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist picks up a wire-service item and republishes it without checking any independent source, trusting the agency entirely — permissible under Article III §4 unless doubt arises.
S-B: The same journalist notices an agency report contains a figure inconsistent with known data; under Article III §4 exception they must now verify in at least one additional independent source before publishing.
S-C: A journalist publishes a story about a government official based solely on a single confidential tip, without seeking a second independent source — a clear violation of Article III §1.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Agency material is treated as pre-verified by the agency; the journalist is not obliged to re-verify it unless doubt arises, at which point one additional independent source suffices (entry #8, Article III §4)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes (legitimate pressures that SHOULD push toward gold pole):
- Information concerns a named individual whose reputation could be harmed by inaccurate reporting
- The story involves criminal allegations where false publication could violate the presumption of innocence
- Competing claims in a politically sensitive story where partial facts could distort reality

Rationalization cues (illegitimate pressures the code warns against):
- Competitor outlet is about to break the same story (deadline / scoop pressure)
- The agency is regarded as generally reliable, so re-checking feels unnecessary even when a discrepancy is apparent
- Story is time-sensitive and a second source is difficult to reach quickly

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The two-independent-source requirement is stated as an unconditional obligation ("je povinný … najmenej v dvoch nezávislých zdrojoch") — the Slovak present indicative form "je povinný" carries a stronger mandatory register than "should verify" phrasing found in many comparable codes. The agency exemption in §4 is a practical carve-out but is explicitly conditioned on absence of doubt, meaning any hesitation triggers the full standard. This combination is stricter than the universal norm.

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. However, the two-source rule creates a particular burden for small local outlets where independent sources on niche topics may be scarce.

source_name: Slovakia Journalist's Code of Ethics (Slovak Syndicate of Journalists)
tension_name: Individual privacy protection vs. public interest disclosure
editorial_dimension: presence of private medical detail
scenario_context: A health-beat story about a city council member whose undisclosed cancer diagnosis was discovered during reporting on a budget vote.
pole_a:
** Publish private information about individuals, or diminish their reputation, whenever the story is sufficiently newsworthy or in the public interest.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support for this as a positive prescription; the code permits it only under defined exceptions.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Do not publish information about an individual's private life without their consent, and never lower their reputation or dignity, except under a narrowly defined public-interest exception with a further sub-exception for suspected unlawful conduct.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article IV §1: consent required; dignity protected even in public-interest reporting unless suspected unlawful conduct is involved)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Novinár nesmie bez súhlasu dotknutej osoby zverejňovať informácie alebo záznamy z jej súkromného života, s výnimkou prípadu, keď ide o vec verejného záujmu. Novinár nesmie znižovať povesť, česť ani dôstojnosť osoby ani pri zverejňovaní informácií a záznamov vo vzťahu k verejnému záujmu, s výnimkou prípadu, keď osoba vzbudzuje podozrenie z protiprávneho konania alebo urážania iných svojím konaním."*
EN gloss: "The journalist must not publish the information or records about the privacy of an individual without the consent of the individual concerned, except in the case of a matter of public interest. The journalist must not lower the reputation, honour or dignity of the individual not even when publishing in relation to a public interest, except the case where the individual raises suspicion of unlawfully acting or causing offence by his or her actions."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist investigating a public official's finances discovers information about the official's medical condition, which the official has not disclosed. Even though the official is a public figure, the medical information concerns private life; publication without consent is prohibited unless the medical condition is directly relevant to the public interest at stake.
S-B: A local politician is credibly suspected of embezzling public funds. The journalist may publish the allegation (public interest exception) but must still protect dignity — reputationally destructive language is only permissible under the further sub-exception that the individual is suspected of unlawful acting (Article IV §1 second sentence).
S-C: A private citizen witnesses a crime and their name appears in a police report. Publishing their name without consent implicates Article IV §1; there is no clear public interest exception unless victim/witness identification itself serves a significant public purpose.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Consent to publish private information is not required when the matter is of public interest (entry #22, Article IV §1 first sentence)
- Reputational harm is permitted (second-level exception) only when the individual is suspected of unlawful acting or causing offence by their actions (entry #22, Article IV §1 second sentence)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- Subject is a public official and the private information relates directly to their exercise of public duties
- The individual is credibly suspected of serious criminal conduct affecting others
- Disclosure serves a protective function for the public (e.g., exposing a dangerous individual)

Rationalization cues:
- Story is commercially compelling or will attract large audiences
- Competitor has published similar private details, creating pressure to match
- Source has provided the information unprompted and the journalist feels it is "already out there"

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The layered exception structure — public interest unlocks publication but does not automatically permit reputational harm; a separate sub-exception is needed — is more protective of individual dignity than many comparable European codes. The Slovak verb "nesmie" (must not) is categorical, not aspirational. The reference to "raising suspicion" rather than conviction or even formal charge creates an intermediate threshold that requires editorial judgment.

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. In small communities, individuals have heightened vulnerability to reputational harm from local reporting, making this tension particularly acute for local journalists.

tension_name: Presumption of innocence vs. transparency about persons suspected of wrongdoing
editorial_dimension: name vs. anonymized reference for a pre-charge suspect
scenario_context: A municipal official is arrested on suspicion of corruption but has not been formally charged, and a local paper reports the arrest.
pole_a:
** Name and identify persons suspected of criminal activity whenever the story is newsworthy, to satisfy public curiosity and accountability norms.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code explicitly opposes this absent the public interest condition.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Respect the presumption of innocence for all persons suspected, accused, or charged; disclose names only when an important public interest specifically justifies naming.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article IV §2)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Novinár rešpektuje prezumpciu neviny vrátane osôb podozrivých zo spáchania trestného činu, obvinených zo spáchania trestného činu alebo obžalovaných zo spáchania trestného činu. Mená ľudí podozrivých z trestnej činnosti sú zverejnené len vtedy, ak zverejnenie ich mien predstavuje dôležitý verejný záujem."*
EN gloss: "The journalist respects the presumption of innocence including persons suspected of committing a crime, accused of committing a crime or charged with a crime. The names of people suspected of criminal activity are disclosed only if releasing their names is an important public interest."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A local official is arrested on suspicion of corruption but has not been charged. A journalist with the official's name considers publishing it. Under Article IV §2, naming is only permitted if an important public interest in disclosure can be identified — not merely because the arrest is newsworthy.
S-B: A public prosecutor is charged with embezzling funds intended for a social welfare programme. The public interest in knowing the identity of the person administering justice is strong; naming is justified under the important public interest standard.
S-C: A private citizen is suspected of a minor financial offence. No public interest in naming can be established; the presumption of innocence norm prevails and the name should be withheld.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Names of suspected persons may be disclosed when releasing them serves an important public interest (entry #23, Article IV §2)
- The definition of "important public interest" (entries #40, #41) constrains and operationalises this exception

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- Subject holds public trust (elected official, prosecutor, police officer) and the suspected conduct relates directly to that role
- Public safety would be served by disclosure (e.g., suspected serial offender whose continued anonymity poses ongoing risk)

Rationalization cues:
- The arrest has been publicly confirmed by police and is therefore treated as "common knowledge," removing felt need to weigh presumption of innocence
- Competitors have already named the person, normalising disclosure
- The story is more compelling with a named individual than an anonymised account

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
Slovak law provides formal presumption-of-innocence protections; the code reinforces these at an ethical level. The phrase "vrátane osôb podozrivých" (including persons suspected) explicitly extends the presumption to the pre-charge stage, which is stricter than some European equivalents that focus primarily on the formally accused. The "important public interest" gateway aligns with Articles V §9–§13 (extraordinary means provisions), suggesting a coherent proportionality framework across the code.

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. Highly relevant in local journalism where named suspects in small communities face severe and lasting reputational harm from even pre-charge reporting.

tension_name: Default transparency in information-gathering vs. covert investigative methods
editorial_dimension: disclosure of covert recording method in the article
scenario_context: An investigative piece on a regional procurement official explains how the reporter obtained the recorded conversation.
pole_a:
** Use covert methods (hidden camera, concealed microphone, false identity, undisclosed recording) whenever they would yield a better or faster story.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code treats covert methods as exceptional and tightly conditional.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Always identify yourself as a journalist, including full name and media affiliation, when gathering information; notify respondents before recording phone calls; use covert methods only when all required conditions are met.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article V §1 establishes the default transparency rule; Articles V §8–§11 define the narrow exception regime)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B (with the L2 exception pathway as the only legitimate route to Pole A)

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Novinár získava textové, zvukové, audiovizuálne a obrazové záznamy a podklady pre články a iné diela spôsobom, z ktorého je zrejmé, že ide o novinára a neskrýva svoje celé meno ani príslušnosť ku konkrétnemu médiu."*
EN gloss: "The journalist acquires text, audio, audiovisual and image recordings and backgrounds for articles and other works in a way that it is clear that he or she is a journalist and does not hide his or her full name or belonging to a specific medium."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist suspects a local official of taking bribes. They attend a meeting with the official while concealing their journalistic identity and using a hidden microphone — without editorial approval and without establishing that ordinary methods could not achieve the same result. This violates Articles V §1, §9, and §10.
S-B: The same journalist, having established that the suspected bribe-taking cannot be documented by open means and having obtained approval at the highest editorial level, uses a concealed microphone at a subsequent meeting. Under Articles V §8–§11, this use is permissible provided it is disclosed to audiences on publication.

pole_a:
** Any editorial decision to restrict, edit, re-frame, or decline to publish constitutes censorship and is therefore forbidden.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code explicitly rejects this reading.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Censorship — defined as restricting or suppressing information for political, economic, or personal reasons — is absolutely forbidden; but editorial management retains legitimate authority over topics, editing, and publication decisions made on journalistic grounds.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article VIII §1–§5: censorship is defined by motive, not by the act of restricting content; editorial authority is affirmed alongside the censorship prohibition)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Cenzúra znamená obmedzenie, úmyselné skreslenie alebo nezverejnenie informácií, zvukových, audiovizuálnych alebo obrazových záznamov, ak k nemu došlo z politických, ekonomických alebo osobných dôvodov. Cenzúra je nezlučiteľná s etickými pravidlami novinárskej práce a je zakázaná."*
EN gloss: "Censorship means a restriction, deliberate misrepresentation or non-disclosure of information, audio, audiovisual or image recordings if it occurred for political, economic or personal reasons. Censorship is incompatible with the ethical rules of journalistic work and it is forbidden."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: An editor kills a story about a major advertiser because they fear the advertiser will withdraw revenue. This is suppression for economic reasons — it meets the definition of censorship under Article VIII §1 and is forbidden.
S-B: An editor kills a story because it fails the two-source verification standard and the journalist cannot obtain a second independent source. This is an editorial quality decision, not motivated by political, economic, or personal reasons — it falls within legitimate editorial authority under Article VIII §3 and is not censorship.
S-C: An editor shortens a piece to fit broadcast time constraints, removing context that the journalist believes is essential. This is "editing" as defined in Article VIII §4–§5 — legitimate editorial management — provided the motivation is journalistic rather than political, economic, or personal.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Editing (semantic, dramaturgical, factual, grammatical, and clarity modifications) is explicitly excluded from the definition of censorship (entry #53, Article VIII §4)
- Editorial management authority (topic selection, processing, publication decision, length, genre, order, context) is explicitly not censorship (entries #52, #54, Article VIII §3–§5)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- The decision to suppress is driven by political loyalty to a party-affiliated owner
- The decision is made to protect an economic partner of the media organisation
- The editor personally benefits from non-disclosure (personal reasons under Article VIII §1)

Rationalization cues:
- The editor characterises a commercially motivated kill as an editorial judgment about story quality
- The journalist characterises routine editing as censorship to resist legitimate quality oversight
- The boundary between "personal reasons" and "editorial judgment" is blurred when the editor is personally acquainted with the subject

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The motivation-based definition of censorship ("z politických, ekonomických alebo osobných dôvodov") is a notable drafting choice: it means the same act (not publishing) can be either censorship or legitimate editorial management depending entirely on why it was done. This creates a significant practical evidentiary challenge — motives are rarely transparent. The Slovak constitutional guarantee of freedom of expression and prohibition on censorship (Article 26 of the Slovak Constitution) operates as a background norm.

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. Local outlets with single-owner structures and advertiser dependency may face this tension more acutely, as economic and personal motivations are harder to separate from editorial judgment.

tension_name: Impartiality and objectivity vs. the right to express opinion and commentary
editorial_dimension: unlabelled opinion embedded in news copy
scenario_context: A municipal politics report on a zoning vote where the reporter's assessment of the decision either bleeds into the news copy or is held out as fact-attributed.
pole_a:
** A journalist's opinion, assessed position, or commentary may freely mix with factual reporting without clear labelling.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code explicitly opposes this.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** All journalistic work must be governed by impartiality, objectivity, and honest verification; where opinion is expressed, it must be clearly labelled as such, distinguished from factual reporting, and grounded in a sufficient factual basis.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article II §2: impartiality and objectivity as governing principles; Article III §8: opinion must be labelled and logically inferred from sufficient factual basis)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Komentáre a názory musia byť jasne označené a odlíšené od správ a faktov. Názory a hodnotenia v komentári musia vychádzať a logicky vyplývať z dostatočného skutkového základu."*
EN gloss: "Comments and opinions must be clearly labelled and distinguished from news and facts. Opinions and assessments made in the commentary must be based on and logically inferred from a sufficient factual basis."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist writes a news report on a local council vote but includes their own assessment that the council's decision was "clearly corrupt" without labelling the assessment as opinion. This violates both the impartiality principle (Article II §2) and the labelling requirement (Article III §8).
S-B: The same journalist publishes a clearly labelled opinion column arguing the council decision was corrupt, citing three specific documented financial relationships as the factual basis. Under Article III §8 this is permissible — the opinion is labelled, distinguished from news, and logically inferred from a sufficient factual basis.
S-C: A journalist writes a commentary with no discernible factual basis, relying entirely on personal political conviction. Even though it is labelled as opinion, it violates Article III §8's requirement that opinions must be logically inferred from a sufficient factual basis.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Subjective assessment and opinion are permitted when clearly labelled, distinguished from news, and grounded in a sufficient factual basis from which they are logically inferable (entry #12, Article III §8)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- Failure to label opinion may mislead audiences into treating personal assessments as verified facts
- In a politically polarised environment, conflating opinion and fact undermines public trust in journalism

Rationalization cues:
- Opinion is commercially attractive and engagement-driving; the distinction between labelled opinion and unlabelled comment is tempting to blur
- The journalist feels strongly about a topic and the opinion bleeds into their news reporting without conscious intent
- Digital formats dissolve the visual separation between news and opinion that print formats traditionally maintained

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The Slovak code's requirement that opinions be "logicky vyplývať z dostatočného skutkového základu" (logically inferred from a sufficient factual basis) is more demanding than codes that require merely that opinions be distinguished from facts. It imposes a substantive quality test on commentary, not just a labelling test. This standard also creates a link between the opinion/fact distinction and the prohibition on publishing known falsehoods (Article III §3).

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. Relevant in local journalism where reporters often have personal relationships with sources and subjects, making neutral distance harder to maintain.

**Supporting extracted principles:** #2, #7, #12

tension_name: Commercial and advertiser interests vs. editorial independence and anti-hidden-advertising duty
editorial_dimension: presence/absence of a paid-content label on commercial copy
scenario_context: A lifestyle section runs a feature on a new rooftop restaurant whose owner is a paying advertiser in the same publication.
pole_a: Accept gifts, sponsored travel, or advertising arrangements without disclosure; allow commercial content to appear as independent journalism; decline to refuse hidden advertising.
pole_b: Refuse gifts or benefits that could compromise impartiality; clearly label all advertising and paid content; disclose third-party-funded expenses to audiences; exercise the right and duty to refuse hidden advertising.

policy_text: Reklamy a platené oznámenia musia byť jasne označené. V prípade komerčného textu nesmie článok vyvolávať dojem, že ide o nezávislú prácu novinára. Novinár a médiá majú právo a povinnosť odmietnuť zverejnenie skrytej reklamy.*

Policy: Reklamy a platené oznámenia musia byť jasne označené. V prípade komerčného textu nesmie článok vyvolávať dojem, že ide o nezávislú prácu novinára. Novinár a médiá majú právo a povinnosť odmietnuť zverejnenie skrytej reklamy.*

Exceptions to this policy:
- Small advertising items and refreshments at press conferences and public events addressed to the public and media representatives are generally acceptable
- Sponsored travel is not prohibited but must be disclosed to audiences
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A company invites a journalist on a sponsored press trip and the journalist publishes a positive travel article without disclosing that the trip was externally funded. This violates Article III §12 (expense disclosure duty) and potentially Article III §11 (gift/benefit acceptance).
Scenario B: An advertiser requests that a paid promotional piece be published without an "advertisement" label, in the same visual format as news articles. The journalist and media are both required to refuse under Article III §9; compliance is not a matter of discretion but a positive duty.
Scenario C: A journalist accepts a bottle of wine from a company they are covering and does not report the gift. If the wine is more than a "small advertising item" as described in the Article III §11 exception, it constitutes a prohibited benefit that may compromise perceived impartiality.

tension_name: Collegial solidarity vs. obligation to expose unethical or unlawful colleagues
editorial_dimension: presence of disclosure of a colleague's misconduct
scenario_context: A media outlet reports on undisclosed political payments to one of its own staff reporters.
pole_a:
** Maintain professional solidarity; do not report on or expose colleagues' misconduct; cooperate with legal proceedings against colleagues only voluntarily.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code explicitly requires the opposite.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Expose and publish the unethical and unlawful actions of colleagues; cooperate as an obligation (not merely a permission) in legal and administrative proceedings related to a colleague's journalistic activity.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article VII §3: positive duty to discover and publish colleagues' misconduct; Article VI §6: obligation to cooperate in legal proceedings)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Novinár má povinnosť odhaľovať a zverejňovať neetické a nezákonné konanie svojich kolegov."*
EN gloss: "The journalist has an obligation to discover and publish the unethical and unlawful actions of his or her colleagues."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist becomes aware that a colleague at the same outlet has been accepting undisclosed payments from a political party in exchange for favourable coverage. Under Article VII §3, the journalist is obliged to expose this — silence or inaction is itself a violation of the code.
S-B: A colleague is subject to a defamation lawsuit arising from their journalistic work. Under Article VI §6, the journalist is obligated to cooperate in the legal proceedings if approached; they cannot refuse on grounds of professional solidarity.
S-C: A journalist suspects a colleague of plagiarism. They have no firm evidence yet. The code's obligation in Article VII §3 is to "discover and publish" — implying an investigative duty, not merely reactive disclosure once evidence is handed to them.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Cooperation in legal proceedings is scoped to proceedings "related to the activity of the journalist" — proceedings unrelated to journalistic work are outside this obligation (entry #46, Article VI §6)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- Undetected colleague misconduct damages the credibility of the entire profession
- The journalistic community's self-regulatory legitimacy depends on internal accountability
- Victims of colleagues' unethical conduct (defamed individuals, plagiarised authors) have a legitimate interest in accountability

Rationalization cues:
- Fear of personal and professional consequences from "naming" a colleague
- Belief that internal informal resolution is preferable to public exposure
- Uncertainty about the threshold of "unethical" and whether the conduct is serious enough to warrant publication

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The positive duty to "odhaľovať a zverejňovať" (discover and publish) rather than merely "report" or "not conceal" is stronger than most comparable codes, which typically frame this as a permission. This framing implies an active investigative posture toward colleagues, not just passive non-obstruction. This is a notable national-specific feature.

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. In small newsrooms, the duty to expose colleagues creates significant personal risk in tightly knit professional communities.

scenarios_block:

tension_name: Protecting vulnerable sources vs. the public's right to complete information
editorial_dimension: identifiability of a minor used as a source
scenario_context: Local coverage of a fatal house fire in which a surviving child witness is quoted and identified.
pole_a:
** Gather and publish all relevant information regardless of the vulnerability of the source, treating all sources equally in the interest of completeness and transparency.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code requires differentiated treatment of vulnerable sources.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Approach vulnerable persons (those inexperienced with media, unaware of consequences, or in difficult life situations, including crime victims, accident witnesses, and minors) with increased sensitivity and responsibility; use minors as sources only in exceptional cases; protect their privacy and legitimate interests unless overridden by public interest; never misuse their trust.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article V §4: increased sensitivity for vulnerable sources; Article V §5: restricted use of minors; Article V §6: privacy and trust protection)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Ľudí, ktorí nie sú skúsení v komunikácii s novinármi, nie sú si vedomí dôsledkov svojho konania alebo sa nachádzajú v mimoriadne ťažkej životnej situácii, predovšetkým obetí alebo svedkov trestných činov, nehôd alebo iných udalostí, ktoré môžu spôsobiť osobe emocionálny stres, novinár pristupuje so zvýšenou citlivosťou a zodpovednosťou."*
EN gloss: "People who are not experienced in communication with journalists, are unaware of the consequences of their actions or find themselves in a particularly difficult life situation, especially victims or witnesses of crimes, accidents or other events that may cause to a person emotional stress, the journalist approaches them with increased sensitivity and responsibility."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A journalist approaches a grieving family member at the scene of a fatal accident and requests an interview. The family member, in emotional distress, agrees. Under Article V §4 the journalist must apply increased sensitivity and responsibility; under Article V §6 they must not misuse the trust placed in them, even if public interest in the story is genuine.
S-B: A 14-year-old witness to a school incident would provide the most compelling account of events. Under Article V §5 the journalist may use the minor as a source only in exceptional circumstances and must give particular regard to their moral and emotional development.
S-C: A crime victim agrees in an emotional moment to have their identity published. Under Article V §6, the journalist's obligation to protect the victim's privacy and legitimate interests is not extinguished simply because consent was given under conditions of distress.

**L2 exceptions:**
- Protection of privacy and legitimate interests of vulnerable persons can be overridden when publication is required for communication of public interest issues — but misuse of trust is never permissible even in public interest cases (entry #34, Article V §6)
- Use of minors as sources is permitted in exceptional cases with regard to moral and emotional development (entry #33, Article V §5)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- Vulnerable individuals are structurally unable to give fully informed consent and may not anticipate long-term consequences of media exposure
- Children's welfare and developmental interests create an independent duty of care beyond ordinary source protection

Rationalization cues:
- The source voluntarily approached the journalist or is willing to speak
- The story is compelling and the vulnerable source provides the most immediate and vivid account
- Competitive pressure to publish before protective instincts take hold

**Cross-linguistic / jurisdictional notes:**
The structure of Article V §6 — "if it is not ruled out for communication of public interest issues" — places the burden of justification on the journalist wishing to override vulnerability protections, rather than on the source to claim protection. This is a notably protective framing. The explicit carve-out that misuse of trust can never be justified, even by public interest, is an absolute prohibition within an otherwise qualified framework.

**Local-news relevance:**
Not addressed explicitly. Local journalists frequently encounter vulnerable sources (accident victims, crime witnesses) in small communities where re-identification is inevitable even from anonymised accounts.

**Supporting extracted principles:** #32, #33, #34

pole_a:
** Allow respondents to correct, suppress, or withhold consent for any part of their interview after the fact, in the interest of maintaining source relationships.
**Pole A provenance:** Inferred — no direct extraction support; the code explicitly rejects post-hoc respondent control beyond narrow citation-level authorisation.

**Pole B (higher / more policy-aligned):** Once a respondent has agreed to disclose information in accordance with the code, the journalist is not obliged to accede to post-hoc correction, suppression, or non-broadcast requests; pre-authorisation agreements are limited to the respondent's own direct citations and may not change meanings or remove answers.
**Pole B provenance:** Directly stated in code (Article V §7)

**Gold (from this source's view):** B

**Suggested policy_text:**
Original: *"Novinár nie je povinný vyhovieť žiadosti respondenta o dodatočnú opravu, nezverejnenie alebo nevysielanie informácií získaných v súlade s týmto Kódexom etiky, pokiaľ respondent predtým súhlasil so zverejnením."*
EN gloss: "The journalist is not obliged to accede to a request from the respondent for additional correction, non-disclosure or non-broadcast of information obtained in accordance with this Code of Ethics as long the respondent has previously agreed to the disclosure."

**Scenarios:**
S-A: A politician gives a recorded interview agreeing to its broadcast. After seeing a transcript they request removal of a damaging answer. Under Article V §7 the journalist is not obliged to comply — the prior consent to disclosure stands and meanings cannot be removed from the original interview.
S-B: Before an interview, a respondent requests full authorisation over the entire article in which their quotes will appear. Under Article V §7 the journalist may not accept such an agreement — authorisation extends only to the respondent's own direct citations, not the surrounding article.
S-C: A pre-interview authorisation agreement is reached. After the interview, the respondent attempts to change the meaning of a quoted statement while accepting the wording. Under Article V §7 this is impermissible — meanings may not be changed under the authorisation process.

**L2 exceptions:**
- A prior authorisation agreement may be accepted in justified cases before the interview begins, but is limited to the respondent's own direct citations; meanings may not be changed and answers may not be removed (entry #35, Article V §7)

**Pressures the code addresses:**
Consensus stakes:
- Post-interview suppression or alteration requests may be motivated by the respondent's desire to hide accurate information from the public
- Allowing meaning-changing authorisation would undermine the factual integrity of the published record

Rationalization cues:
- Acceding to the respondent's request preserves the ongoing source relationship and future access
- The journalist fears the respondent will complain to management or take legal action

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A politician gives a recorded interview agreeing to its broadcast. After seeing a transcript they request removal of a damaging answer. Under Article V §7 the journalist is not obliged to comply — the prior consent to disclosure stands and meanings cannot be removed from the original interview.
Scenario B: Before an interview, a respondent requests full authorisation over the entire article in which their quotes will appear. Under Article V §7 the journalist may not accept such an agreement — authorisation extends only to the respondent's own direct citations, not the surrounding article.
Scenario C: A pre-interview authorisation agreement is reached. After the interview, the respondent attempts to change the meaning of a quoted statement while accepting the wording. Under Article V §7 this is impermissible — meanings may not be changed under the authorisation process.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The highest and primary obligation of ethical journalism is to serve the public. / Avoid conflicts of interest, real or perceived. Disclose unavoidable conflicts. / Refuse gifts, favors, fees, free travel and special treatment. / Deny favored treatment to advertisers, donors or any other special interests, and resist internal and external pressure to influence coverage. / Distinguish news from advertising and shun hybrids that blur the lines between the two. Prominently label sponsored content.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Unavoidable conflicts must be disclosed rather than simply avoided
- Sponsored content is permissible but must be prominently labelled
- No de minimis or threshold exception stated for gifts
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A local journalist accepts a free press trip from a tourism board and then writes a travel feature about the destination without disclosing the free travel or labelling the content as sponsored.
Scenario B: An editor's publisher tells her to soften a critical story about a major advertiser; she refuses, discloses the pressure to her editor-in-chief, and publishes the story as reported.
Scenario C: A reporter is offered exclusive access and documents by a source in exchange for a guarantee of favourable coverage; she declines the arrangement, pursues the story through independent reporting, and discloses the offer.

Policy: Avoid pandering to lurid curiosity, even if others do. / Balance the public's need for information against potential harm or discomfort.

- The balancing test against genuine public need may justify disturbing content in some circumstances
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Policy: News organisations must consider themselves as special socio-economic agencies whose entrepreneurial objectives have to be limited by the conditions for providing access to a fundamental right. / the media should exploit neither the quality nor the substance of the news or opinions for purposes of boosting readership or audience figures in order to increase advertising revenue. / Neither publishers and proprietors nor journalists should consider that they own the news.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An editor selects which stories to cover based primarily on predicted click-through rates and advertising yield, deprioritising important but low-traffic public-affairs stories.

tension_name: Proprietorial Editorial Authority vs. Journalist Internal Freedom
editorial_dimension: presence of ownership-disclosure clause

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: in addition to safeguarding the freedom of the media, freedom within the media must also be protected and internal pressures guarded against. / the legitimate respect for publishers' and owners' ideological orientations is limited by the absolute requirements on truthful news reporting and ethical opinions. / rules must be drawn up for editorial staff in order to regulate professional relations between the journalists and the publishers and proprietors within the media, separately from the normal requirements of labour relations.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Owners' ideological orientations are legitimate *unless* they override truthful news reporting or ethical opinions (Entry #18) — the code acknowledges owner authority while strictly limiting its scope.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A proprietor instructs journalists not to report on a story that would damage a business partner, invoking the owner's editorial prerogative; no editorial rules exist to allow journalists to resist this instruction.
Scenario B: An editorial board established under formalised editorial rules challenges a publisher's directive to shade coverage of an election in a particular direction, invoking the outlet's publicly stated ethical commitments.
Scenario C: A journalist invokes the conscience clause when ordered to produce content that conflicts with verified facts, but finds no legal or contractual mechanism exists to protect them from dismissal.

Policy: It would be wrong to infer from the importance of this role that the media actually represent public opinion or that they should replace the specific functions of the public authorities or institutions of an educational or cultural character such as schools. / This would amount to transforming the media and journalism into authorities or counter-authorities ('mediocracy'), even though they would not be representative of the citizens or subject to the same democratic controls as the public authorities.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A major news outlet declares itself the "voice of the people" and conducts a sustained campaign to oust an elected official, framing the campaign as giving expression to public opinion that democratic processes have failed to register.
Scenario B: A journalist reports on a policy failure and calls for legislative accountability, providing citizens with the information they need to form their own demands of elected representatives, without itself substituting for the democratic process.
Scenario C: A media organisation establishes a regular "citizens' court" format in which public figures are tried by journalists and audience verdict, presenting this as a democratic accountability mechanism outside the formal judicial system.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: we must legally expand and clarify the nature of the conscience clause and professional secrecy vis-a-vis confidential sources, harmonising national provisions on this matter so that they can be implemented in the wider context of democratic Europe.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The verification requirement (Entry #5) creates a structural tension: verification may require corroboration that identifies sources, while confidentiality requires non-disclosure. The code does not explicitly resolve this.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes allegations of institutional wrongdoing from an anonymous source; the audience cannot verify the source's credibility or potential agenda, but the journalist is bound by professional secrecy not to reveal the source's identity.
Scenario B: A journalist refuses to identify a confidential source even when a court orders disclosure, invoking professional secrecy — but must weigh this against the source's potential to mislead audiences if their interests are undisclosed.
Scenario C: A journalist verifies information through multiple independent sources but reports only the information, not the sources, leaving the audience unable to assess the evidentiary basis independently.

Policy: self-regulatory bodies or mechanisms must be set up comprising publishers, journalists, media users' associations, experts from the academic world and judges; they will be responsible for issuing resolutions on respect for ethical precepts in journalism, with prior commitment on the part of the media to publish the relevant resolutions. / The self-regulatory bodies or mechanisms, the media users' associations and the relevant university departments could publish each year the research done a posteriori on the truthfulness of the information broadcast by the media, comparing the news with the actual facts.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A media organisation participates in a self-regulatory body but refuses to publish its adverse rulings, treating them as confidential internal documents.
Scenario B: An outlet publicly commits in advance to publishing all self-regulatory body rulings, including adverse ones, and does so when a ruling finds against them on a factual accuracy complaint.
Scenario C: A self-regulatory body is established but includes only publishers and senior editors, excluding journalists' associations, media users, and independent experts, resulting in an accountability mechanism captured by proprietorial interests.

tension_name: Publication Speed and Editorial Independence vs. Correction and Right of Reply
editorial_dimension: presence vs. absence of a prompt, full correction of an erroneous report
scenario_context: A local newspaper that wrongly named a shopkeeper as a fraud suspect addresses the error after the shopkeeper requests a correction.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Correction is triggered by a request from the persons concerned (Entry #32) — it is not necessarily automatic in the absence of a request, though the code's overall truthfulness norms would support proactive correction.
- National legislation should provide sanctions and, where applicable, compensation (Entry #32).
- Right of reply should be harmonised across Council of Europe member states per Resolution (74) 26 (Entry #33).
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes an erroneous report about an individual; the individual requests a correction; the outlet publishes a brief, buried clarification weeks later that does not provide the full relevant information.
Scenario B: A news outlet, upon receiving a correction request from a named individual, publishes a prompt, prominent correction with full context in the same position and format as the original story.
Scenario C: An editor refuses a right-of-reply request from a named subject of a story on the grounds that the outlet's editorial line is confirmed by the story and no obligation to provide a reply exists.

policy_text: Professional secrecy is a journalist's right, as well as a duty that guarantees the confidentiality of information sources. Consequently, journalists shall guarantee the right of their information sources to remain anonymous, if so requested.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Professional secrecy is a journalist's right, as well as a duty that guarantees the confidentiality of information sources. Consequently, journalists shall guarantee the right of their information sources to remain anonymous, if so requested.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Source has knowingly misrepresented information, and this is reliably established
- Disclosure is the only means to avoid serious and immediate harm to persons
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A source provides false information that leads to publication of an inaccurate story. The journalist learns the source deliberately fabricated the claim. The code permits — but does not require — revealing the source's identity once the misrepresentation is "reliably stated."
Scenario B: A confidential source reveals information about an imminent violent act. Disclosure of the source's identity is the only available means to prevent the harm. The code permits disclosure under the "serious and immediate harm" exception.
Scenario C: No such threshold is met — the source's information is accurate and no harm is threatened. The journalist must maintain confidentiality regardless of institutional pressure, competitive interest, or editorial convenience.

policy_text: Without prejudice to protecting the right of citizens to be informed, the journalist shall respect the right of persons to their own privacy and image. … Defence of the public interest alone justifies intrusion or inquiry into a person's private life without his or her prior consent.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Without prejudice to protecting the right of citizens to be informed, the journalist shall respect the right of persons to their own privacy and image. … Defence of the public interest alone justifies intrusion or inquiry into a person's private life without his or her prior consent.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Defence of the public interest justifies intrusion without prior consent
- Tighter default for hospitalised persons — institutional context raises the threshold
- Extra-tight ("extreme rigour") rules apply to minors in criminal or privacy matters
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist investigates the health of a public official and publishes details of the official's hospitalisation. The code requires "particular care" and demands a demonstrable public-interest justification beyond the official's public role (§4(d)).
Scenario B: A news outlet publishes photographs of minor children involved peripherally in a crime story. The code requires "extreme rigour" and, for minors in criminal or privacy-adjacent matters, prohibits interviewing, photographing, or recording them (§6).
Scenario C: A journalist obtains information about a private individual's personal life that is embarrassing but has no bearing on any public interest. Publishing would serve curiosity or entertainment; the code does not permit this intrusion (§4(a)).

scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist reports on a high-profile arrest and is tempted to name the suspect's spouse and adult children, who are known in the community. The code requires withholding those names unless naming them is necessary for the story to be complete or fair (§5(a)).

Policy: The criteria indicated in the above two principles shall be applied with extreme rigour when the coverage may affect minors. In particular, the journalist shall refrain from interviewing, photographing or recording minors with regard to matters relating to criminal activities or those which can be considered to fall within the field of privacy.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The code states no explicit exception to the prohibition on interviewing, photographing, or recording minors in criminal or privacy matters. The §6 prohibition is the most absolute-sounding rule in the entire code.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Police release information about a juvenile offender. A journalist wishes to interview the minor at the youth detention facility and photograph them. The code prohibits this regardless of public interest in the case (§6).
Scenario B: A minor is peripherally identified in court documents as a witness to a crime. A journalist considers publishing identifying details. The code requires not publishing material that could identify the minor (§§5(b), 6).
Scenario C: A child is featured in a human-interest story about poverty. Because this touches on matters "within the field of privacy," the code requires special attention and may prohibit recording without heightened justification (§§4(e), 6).

policy_text: The right to invoke the conscience clause, if the media on which they rely claims a moral attitude that damages their professional dignity or substantively alters the editorial stance.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The right to invoke the conscience clause, if the media on which they rely claims a moral attitude that damages their professional dignity or substantively alters the editorial stance.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The conscience clause is triggered when the media claims a "moral attitude that damages professional dignity" OR "substantively alters the editorial stance" — two distinct triggers
- Freedom of information must be compatible with the rights of the media in which the news is expressed — this condition acknowledges some legitimate employer authority
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An owner instructs a journalist to write a story framed in a way the journalist believes crosses the line from editorial viewpoint into paid promotion. The journalist may invoke the conscience clause (§II-1(d)) and is entitled to protection under §II-2.
Scenario B: A media conglomerate acquires a newspaper and substantially changes its editorial line. A journalist whose professional identity was built around the original stance may invoke the conscience clause (§II-1(d)).
Scenario C: An advertiser pressures an editor to kill a story. The journalist is entitled to resist that pressure and to seek protection from associations or institutional organisations (§II-2).

policy_text: The commitment to the search for truth shall always lead journalists to report only on facts of whose origin they are certain… They must substantiate the information they circulate, including the duty to compare sources and to give the person concerned the opportunity to offer his or her own version of the facts.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The commitment to the search for truth shall always lead journalists to report only on facts of whose origin they are certain… They must substantiate the information they circulate, including the duty to compare sources and to give the person concerned the opportunity to offer his or her own version of the facts.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Breaking news arrives from a single source during a developing incident. The code requires that the journalist not publish until the origin is certain or, where urgency requires partial publication, that errors be corrected immediately in equivalent format (§§III-1, III-1(b)).
Scenario B: A journalist writes a profile of a company based on documents from one source. The code requires comparing sources and giving the company the opportunity to provide its own version before publication (§III-1(a)).
Scenario C: A published story contains a factual error. A brief correction buried in the paper's corrections column does not satisfy the code; the correction must use the same typographical or audiovisual format as the original story (§III-1(b)).

policy_text: With the same exceptions provided for professional secrecy, the journalist shall respect the off the record rule if it has been expressly invoked or it is concluded that such was the will of the informant.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: With the same exceptions provided for professional secrecy, the journalist shall respect the off the record rule if it has been expressly invoked or it is concluded that such was the will of the informant.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The same two exceptions that apply to professional secrecy apply to the off-the-record rule: knowing source misrepresentation and preventing serious/immediate harm
- The right not to provide information exists "without prejudice" to the journalist's professional duty to address citizens' right to information — the code does not resolve this tension but acknowledges it
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A source provides sensitive information in a context where no explicit off-the-record designation was made, but the circumstances imply confidentiality. The code requires the journalist to infer and honour the source's likely intent (§III-4).
Scenario B: A politician declines to answer a journalist's questions. The code prohibits harassment or coercion; the journalist may pursue the story through other means but must respect the refusal (§III-3).
Scenario C: A source who provided off-the-record information later misrepresents what they said publicly. The professional-secrecy exceptions apply: if the source has "knowingly misrepresented information," the journalist may consider disclosure (§§III-4, II-3).

tension_name: Editorial viewpoint and non-neutrality vs. clear fact/opinion distinction
editorial_dimension: blending of reporter interpretation into a factual account vs. labelling it as analysis
scenario_context: A city-hall report on a budget vote where the reporter's assessment of the mayor's motive risks being read as established fact.
pole_a: Express editorial viewpoints, interpretations, and critical opinions without necessarily maintaining a clear formal boundary between those opinions and reported facts.
pole_b: Always make a clear and unequivocal distinction between reported facts and opinions, interpretations, or conjecture — while retaining full freedom not to be neutral.
text_pole_a: The city council approved the $4.2 million arena subsidy on Tuesday, a move Mayor Daniel Ortega pushed through to shore up support among the developers funding his re-election bid.
text_pole_b: The city council approved the $4.2 million arena subsidy on Tuesday, a move that, in this reporter's analysis, helps Mayor Daniel Ortega court the developers funding his re-election bid.
diff_span_pole_a: a move Mayor Daniel Ortega pushed through to shore up support among the developers funding his re-election bid
diff_span_pole_b: a move that, in this reporter's analysis, helps Mayor Daniel Ortega court the developers funding his re-election bid
policy_text: Journalists shall always make a clear and unequivocal distinction between the facts they recount and what may be opinions, interpretations or conjecture, although in the exercise of their professional activity they are not obliged to be neutral.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Journalists shall always make a clear and unequivocal distinction between the facts they recount and what may be opinions, interpretations or conjecture, although in the exercise of their professional activity they are not obliged to be neutral.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The journalist is expressly not obliged to be neutral — this is a permission, not an exception to the fact/opinion rule
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist covers a political controversy and weaves their interpretation of motives into what is presented as a factual account. The code requires separating these layers clearly, even if the journalist holds a firm editorial view (§III-5).
Scenario B: An opinion column labels a public figure's action as "corrupt" without distinguishing this characterisation from established facts. The code requires the journalist to make explicit whether this is interpretation or proven fact (§§III-1, III-5).
Scenario C: A news report accurately presents facts but buries a strong editorial conclusion in the final paragraph without labelling it as opinion. The code's "clear and unequivocal" standard is not met even if the journalist's overall stance is legitimate.

policy_block:

- The financial conflicts provisions (§§III-8(a–c)) include the temporal qualifier "near future" in §III-8(c), which is undefined
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A technology company offers a journalist a fully paid trip to a product launch in exchange for coverage. The code prohibits acceptance as a gratuity from a third party that influences published content (§III-7).

Policy: In the performance of their professional duties, journalists shall use justifiable methods to obtain news, which excludes unlawful procedures.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

policy_text: Not to publish information, documents, images or sound recordings of which the origin is unknown to the journalist. / If information is unconfirmed to clearly say so. / Not to suppress information or any essential elements of a story.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Not to publish information, documents, images or sound recordings of which the origin is unknown to the journalist. / If information is unconfirmed to clearly say so. / Not to suppress information or any essential elements of a story.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist receives an anonymously leaked document that is highly newsworthy. The source cannot be identified. Under Pole A, the journalist publishes immediately because the public interest is urgent and a competitor may break the story first.
Scenario B: The same journalist holds the document, works to establish its origin, and — if unable to do so before publication deadline — either withholds it or explicitly labels its provenance as unverifiable, in line with art. 03.
Scenario C: Breaking news of a catastrophe produces chaotic early reports. The journalist publishes initial facts with clear "unconfirmed" labels rather than either suppressing the story entirely or presenting speculation as established fact.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: To respect peoples' privacy in so far as the public interest does not demand otherwise. / To disregard anonymous or unfounded accusations. / To seek out the truth, in the interests of the public's right to know, whatever the consequences to him- or herself.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Privacy protection relaxes when public interest demands otherwise. The code does not define "public interest," leaving interpretive discretion to the journalist and, ultimately, the Press Council.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist investigating a private individual's financial dealings publishes details about their family circumstances because they are technically true and add colour to the story, without assessing whether any genuine public interest is served.
Scenario B: The same journalist applies the public-interest test: the financial dealings of the individual, who holds a public procurement role, are reportable; the domestic details are withheld because no public-interest necessity exists.
Scenario C: An anonymous tip alleges serious misconduct by a named private person. The journalist neither publishes the allegation immediately (which would violate the no-anonymous-accusation rule) nor ignores it entirely (which could suppress an essential story), but pursues corroboration before reporting.

Policy: In respecting human dignity, the journalist must avoid any allusion by text, image or sound to a person's ethnic or national origin, religion, gender, sexual orientation as well as to any illness or physical or mental handicap that could be discriminatory in character. / The reporting of war, acts of terrorism, accidents and catastrophes by means of text, image and sound should respect the victims' suffering and the feelings of their loved ones.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: Coverage of a mass-casualty event includes graphic photographs of the dead and identifies victims by religion and ethnicity in a way that implies causal linkage without evidence, maximising the emotional and informational impact of the story.
Scenario B: The journalist reports the same event accurately but selects images that convey the gravity of the situation without gratuitous depiction of individual suffering; personal characteristics are mentioned only where directly relevant to explaining the event.
Scenario C: A crime story involves a perpetrator whose mental health history is publicly documented. The journalist must decide whether mentioning it is discriminatory (in violation of art. 08) or essential context (art. 03 no-suppression duty) — the code's silence on the threshold between "clearly relevant" and "discriminatory" leaves this a genuine judgment call.

policy_text: Not to use dishonest methods to obtain information, recordings, images or documents. / Not to manipulate them, or have them manipulated by a third party with a view to falsification.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Not to use dishonest methods to obtain information, recordings, images or documents. / Not to manipulate them, or have them manipulated by a third party with a view to falsification.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist investigating food-safety violations poses as a restaurant employee over several weeks to gather footage. The deception is the only practical means of obtaining evidence. Under Pole A, the public-interest value of the story justifies the method.
Scenario B: The same journalist recognises that the code as written contains no public-interest exception for undercover methods and declines the approach, seeking documentary evidence and whistleblower testimony instead.
Scenario C: A journalist receives authentic footage of misconduct but is offered an edited version that is more dramatic. Accepting and publishing the edited version — even if the original is genuine — would violate art. 04's prohibition on having material manipulated with a view to falsification.

policy_text: To respect professional secrecy and not reveal the source of any information obtained in confidence.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: To respect professional secrecy and not reveal the source of any information obtained in confidence.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A whistleblower's identity would, if disclosed, add significant credibility to an allegation of serious corruption and might itself constitute newsworthy information (e.g., a very senior official). Under Pole A, the journalist considers whether the public-interest value of disclosure outweighs the confidence given.
Scenario B: The same journalist treats the confidence as inviolable regardless of the credibility benefit of disclosure, consistent with art. 06.
Scenario C: A journalist discovers that a confidential source has themselves been misleading the journalist. The code is silent on whether deception by a source releases the journalist from confidentiality — under the art. 06 formulation, the duty appears to persist.

policy_text: To take journalistic directives only from designated editorial superiors; and to respect those directives only when they are not contrary to this declaration. / The right not to act in any way nor express any opinion that is contrary to professional rules or personal conscience. policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: To take journalistic directives only from designated editorial superiors; and to respect those directives only when they are not contrary to this declaration. / The right not to act in any way nor express any opinion that is contrary to professional rules or personal conscience. As a result, journalists should not suffer any prejudice.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Obedience to editorial directives is suspended when those directives conflict with the Declaration.
- The right to refuse directives contrary to stated organisational policy applies only when that policy was communicated in writing before employment and has not been lawfully modified.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An editor instructs a journalist to publish a story that the journalist believes violates the privacy provisions of art. 07. The journalist complies because refusing could jeopardise employment.
Scenario B: The same journalist invokes art. 11 / Rights art. 02 to refuse the directive, is protected from prejudice by the Declaration, and escalates through professional channels or to the Press Council.
Scenario C: An owner attempts to change the editorial policy mid-contract without the journalist's agreement. The journalist invokes Rights art. 03: since the policy was communicated in writing before employment and cannot be revoked unilaterally, the directive is illegitimate and the journalist may refuse it without breach on their part.
