policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: To take journalistic directives only from designated editorial superiors; and to respect those directives only when they are not contrary to this declaration. / The right not to act in any way nor express any opinion that is contrary to professional rules or personal conscience. As a result, journalists should not suffer any prejudice.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Obedience to editorial directives is suspended when those directives conflict with the Declaration.
- The right to refuse directives contrary to stated organisational policy applies only when that policy was communicated in writing before employment and has not been lawfully modified.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An editor instructs a journalist to publish a story that the journalist believes violates the privacy provisions of art. 07. The journalist complies because refusing could jeopardise employment.
Scenario B: The same journalist invokes art. 11 / Rights art. 02 to refuse the directive, is protected from prejudice by the Declaration, and escalates through professional channels or to the Press Council.
Scenario C: An owner attempts to change the editorial policy mid-contract without the journalist's agreement. The journalist invokes Rights art. 03: since the policy was communicated in writing before employment and cannot be revoked unilaterally, the directive is illegitimate and the journalist may refuse it without breach on their part.

pole_b: Use entertainment and creative programming deliberately and intentionally to elevate dialogue on important social issues and generate positive cultural and social impact.

policy_text: We understand that our entertainment programming can have an impact on culture. Below are recent examples of the ways in which we have elevated the dialogue on important social issues through our creative programming and initiatives.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: We understand that our entertainment programming can have an impact on culture. Below are recent examples of the ways in which we have elevated the dialogue on important social issues through our creative programming and initiatives.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The code limits the explicit social-impact mandate to "entertainment programming" and "creative programming and initiatives," which may implicitly carve out news reporting as a separate domain not subject to the social-elevation directive. However, this carve-out is not made explicit.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A CNN documentary team is told by senior producers that their film should "elevate the dialogue" on a specific social issue identified as a company priority; a staff journalist objects that this constitutes editorial agenda-setting incompatible with neutral fact-reporting.
Scenario B: An entertainment division commissions a drama series designed to shift public opinion on a health-policy debate; the news division asks whether the same company's journalists can cover that debate neutrally given the company's stated intent to shape cultural outcomes.
Scenario C: The "Responsible Content" team selects which social issues are "important" enough to merit programming elevation; journalists question by what standard that selection is made and whether issues not selected are thereby rendered less legitimate.

tension_name: Monitoring discriminatory media content vs. freedom of expression and press freedom
editorial_dimension: framing of monitoring as rights-protection vs. censorship
scenario_context: A report on an advertising self-regulatory body reviewing the portrayal of women in billboard campaigns.

pole_b: Monitoring mechanisms should be established to identify images that are discriminatory or that violate women's and children's rights across all media formats — including online, advertising, marketing, and entertainment — provided such mechanisms are anchored in human rights and dignity rather than censorship.
text_pole_a: The Advertising Standards Council launched a programme this week to review the depiction of women in outdoor campaigns, a move several agencies described as a threat to creative freedom and free expression.
text_pole_b: The Advertising Standards Council launched a programme this week to review the depiction of women in outdoor campaigns, a move the council said is grounded in human rights and dignity rather than restriction of speech.
diff_span_pole_a: a move several agencies described as a threat to creative freedom and free expression
diff_span_pole_b: a move the council said is grounded in human rights and dignity rather than restriction of speech
policy_text: Urge the definition of ethical guidelines adapted to all types of media, including on-line technologies and virtual reality, as well as monitoring mechanisms with respect to images that are discriminatory or that violate children's and women's rights in information, advertisements, marketing, and entertainment; this not with a mind to restrain freedom of expression and of the press, but rather to ensure the respect of human rights and dignity.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Urge the definition of ethical guidelines adapted to all types of media, including on-line technologies and virtual reality, as well as monitoring mechanisms with respect to images that are discriminatory or that violate children's and women's rights in information, advertisements, marketing, and entertainment; this not with a mind to restrain freedom of expression and of the press, but rather to ensure the respect of human rights and dignity.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Monitoring must be framed around human rights and dignity, not censorship
- Monitoring must not restrain freedom of expression or press freedom
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A media outlet resists participation in a gender-portrayal monitoring body on the grounds that any external review of content constitutes an infringement on editorial independence and freedom of the press.
Scenario B: An industry self-regulatory council establishes a content-monitoring framework that tracks frequency and type of sexualised images of women across advertising and news, reporting findings publicly without imposing prior restraint or compelled take-down.
Scenario C: A government agency attempts to administer a discriminatory-images monitoring programme over media industry objections; the code's framing — human rights rationale, not censorship — and the principle that governments should not define journalistic ethics together surface the sharpest version of this tension.

tension_name: Affirmative structural intervention for gender equity vs. editorial and hiring autonomy

policy_block:

Policy: No one shall be declared 'guilty' unless it is determined by the judicial system. / Acts considered as crime according to the law cannot be attributed to anyone unless there are reasonable reasons to believe that it is true.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The journalist avoids publishing which is violent, hateful, tyrannical and encouraging discrimination, and harming humanitarian values.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist covering a terrorist attack publishes graphic footage to convey the full horror of the event and deter complacency. The content is violent; the public-interest justification is strong but the code as written does not supply an exception.
Scenario B: A reporter investigates a neo-Nazi group and quotes extensively from their literature to document the ideology's spread. The quoted content is hateful and discriminatory. Entry #18 would prohibit publishing it, but accuracy and the public's right to know pull toward inclusion.
Scenario C: A news outlet broadcasts footage of a lynching shared on social media to report on mob violence. The footage is both violent and newsworthy. The code's rule and the accuracy obligation are directly in conflict; the code provides no resolution.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: These qualifications of publications, which are announcements and advertisements in nature, are stated in a way that leaves no room for doubt.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: An outlet publishes a branded-content piece about a local business formatted identically to a news story, with no label. This violates entry #19 directly.
Scenario B: A political party purchases space for an announcement; the outlet labels it "Announcement" in a small font. Whether this "leaves no room for doubt" is a judgment call the code's absolute language leaves open.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: The mass media and those who control or serve them, as well as all organized groups within national communities, are urged—with due regard to the principles embodied in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, particularly the principle of freedom of expression—to promote understanding, tolerance and friendship among individuals and groups and to contribute to the eradication of racism, racial discrimination and racial prejudice, in particular by refraining from presenting a stereotyped, partial, unilateral or tendentious picture of individuals and of various human groups.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The active promotion duty applies "with due regard to the principles embodied in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, particularly the principle of freedom of expression" — freedom of expression is acknowledged as a qualifying principle.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist covering urban crime statistics presents data broken down by ethnicity without contextual analysis, attributing no cause and offering no structural frame — treating the numbers as self-evidently neutral.
Scenario B: A journalist covering the same statistics contextualises them with historical, economic, and social factors consistent with Entry #5, names the structural dimensions of racial inequality consistent with Entry #8, and explicitly declines to present the figures as evidence of group-level inferiority.
Scenario C: A broadcaster debates whether to run a segment that "presents both sides" of a scientific study purporting to show racial cognitive differences — the Declaration's framework would treat amplifying that study without scientific and ethical counter-framing as a failure of the media's active duty.

policy_text: Any theory which involves the claim that racial or ethnic groups are inherently superior or inferior, thus implying that some would be entitled to dominate or eliminate others, presumed to be inferior, or which bases value judgments on racial differentiation, has no scientific foundation and is contrary to the moral and ethical principles of humanity.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Any theory which involves the claim that racial or ethnic groups are inherently superior or inferior, thus implying that some would be entitled to dominate or eliminate others, presumed to be inferior, or which bases value judgments on racial differentiation, has no scientific foundation and is contrary to the moral and ethical principles of humanity.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Freedom of expression is acknowledged as a qualifying principle in the media-conduct provisions, creating genuine tension with the absolute prohibition on racial-superiority theories in entries #6 and #7.
- The prohibition is stated in absolute terms ("has no scientific foundation and is contrary to the moral and ethical principles of humanity") with no exceptions for context, historical commentary, or academic debate.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist publishes an interview with a researcher who claims genetic data supports cognitive differences between racial groups, presenting the researcher's claims without challenge as a legitimate scientific controversy.
Scenario B: A journalist reporting on the same researcher contextualises the claims against the Declaration's finding that such theories have no scientific foundation, consults interdisciplinary counter-sources per Entry #30, and explains clearly why the research methodology has been rejected by the scientific community.
Scenario C: An editor declines to run a column arguing that historical colonial hierarchies reflect natural group differences, citing both the Declaration's absolute rejection of racial value judgments and the legal framework endorsed in Entry #27.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Where circumstances warrant, special programmes should be undertaken to promote the advancement of disadvantaged groups and, in the case of nationals, to ensure their effective participation in the decision-making processes of the community.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Special programmes are warranted only "where circumstances warrant" — they are not universally mandatory, creating an evidential threshold
- Measures must not "appear racially discriminatory themselves"
- For decision-making participation, the provision applies specifically to nationals

Policy: It is, in particular, incumbent upon such specialists to ensure, by all means available to them, that their research findings are not misinterpreted, and also that they assist the public in understanding such findings.

policy_text: Population groups of foreign origin, particularly migrant workers and their families who contribute to the development of the host country, should benefit from appropriate measures designed to afford them security and respect for their dignity and cultural values and to facilitate their adaptation to the host environment and their professional advancement with a view to their subsequent reintegration in their country of origin and their contribution to its development.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Population groups of foreign origin, particularly migrant workers and their families who contribute to the development of the host country, should benefit from appropriate measures designed to afford them security and respect for their dignity and cultural values and to facilitate their adaptation to the host environment and their professional advancement with a view to their subsequent reintegration in their country of origin and their contribution to its development.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Coverage must also acknowledge the adaptation dimension — the Declaration supports measures facilitating migrants' adaptation to the host environment
- The framework applies particularly to migrant workers who contribute to the host country's development, which could be read as conditioning dignity entitlements on economic contribution — though this reading is inconsistent with the Declaration's broader dignity-for-all framework in Entry #1
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A news channel runs a primetime package on immigration framed entirely around border enforcement, crime statistics attributed to foreign nationals, and strain on public services, with no voice given to migrant community organisations or acknowledgment of labour-market contributions.
Scenario B: A journalist covering the same immigration debate ensures migrant workers and their community associations are given full voice consistent with Entry #19's reciprocity requirement, includes data on economic and developmental contributions, and contextualises crime statistics against the general population baseline.
Scenario C: A reporter covering a local school's decision not to offer mother-tongue classes to the children of migrant families frames it as a question of educational rights under Entry #34, rather than solely as a resource or integration debate.

tension_name: Child protection from harm vs. public interest / newsworthiness
editorial_dimension: identifiability of an at-risk child witness
scenario_context: Coverage of a humanitarian crisis where a child gang-violence witness could be exposed to retaliation if identified.

policy_text: Do not publish a story or an image which might put the child, siblings or peers at risk even when identities are changed, obscured or not used. / When in doubt about whether a child is at risk, report on the general situation for children rather than on an individual child, no matter how newsworthy the story.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Do not publish a story or an image which might put the child, siblings or peers at risk even when identities are changed, obscured or not used. / When in doubt about whether a child is at risk, report on the general situation for children rather than on an individual child, no matter how newsworthy the story.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The no-publish rule applies even when identities are changed, obscured, or not used — the test is the risk from the content itself, not merely identity disclosure
- The default-to-general-reporting rule applies specifically "when in doubt" — where risk is clearly assessed as absent, the rule may not apply in the same absolute form
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist obtains footage of a named child in a war zone that would powerfully illustrate a major humanitarian crisis. Publishing would inform millions but could expose the child to retribution from armed groups. Pole-A reasoning: the public interest is overwhelming and identity can be obscured. Pole-B reasoning: the code requires withholding even when identities are obscured if content itself creates risk.
Scenario B: A reporter is uncertain whether a refugee child's story would endanger the child's family still in the country of origin. The story is timely and would drive policy change. The code directs the journalist to report on the general refugee situation for children rather than this individual child.
Scenario C: A child's testimony is the only first-hand account of a massacre. Publishing it would serve accountability journalism; not publishing it leaves perpetrators unidentified. The code's precautionary principle applies: potential harm to the child takes precedence over newsworthiness.

policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Ensure that the child would not be endangered or adversely affected by showing their home, community or general whereabouts. / Always provide an accurate context for the child's story or image.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The accurate-context requirement is unqualified but must be read alongside entry #18's safety constraint — context that endangers the child cannot be "accurate context" in the code's framework.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist photographs a child in a specific village to document drought conditions. The village name and region would help international audiences understand the geography of the crisis, but armed groups are known to operate in that area and the image could help identify the child's family. The code requires withholding the location detail.
Scenario B: A news segment interviews a child refugee. The visual background of a recognisable camp or landmark would give audiences important context but could allow hostile actors to locate the child's family in the country of origin. The code requires the journalist to consider what the background "might imply" and to ensure location does not endanger the child.
Scenario C: A story about child labour in a specific factory district would be most powerful if the exact neighbourhood is named. Doing so could expose the individual child interviewees to employer retaliation. The code requires the journalist to weigh this risk and to omit or generalise geographic references if harm is possible.

The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: When trying to determine the best interests of a child, the child's right to have their views taken into account are to be given due weight in accordance with their age and maturity. / Obtain permission from the child and his or her guardian for all interviews, videotaping and, when possible, for documentary photographs.

Exceptions to this policy:
- Weight given to child's views increases with age and maturity — younger children's views carry less independent weight
- Consent must be made "in consultation with an adult the child trusts" — not necessarily a legal guardian
- Child who initiates contact to exercise freedom of expression represents a case where child agency is particularly strong
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A guardian consents to their child being interviewed about a traumatic experience that the child visibly does not want to discuss. Guardian consent is present; the child's distress is not. The code requires that the child's own views be given weight — a willing guardian does not override an unwilling child.
Scenario B: A mature teenager initiates contact with a journalist, wanting to publicly describe abuse by a family member. The guardian (the alleged abuser) would not consent. The code's entry #28 (child-initiated expression) and entry #6 (child's views weighted by age and maturity) together suggest the child's autonomous choice carries significant weight, though the code does not resolve this conflict explicitly.
Scenario C: A young child is coached by a guardian to tell a particular version of events. The code's anti-staging rule and the instruction to consult "those closest to the child" beyond just guardians indicate that guardian direction alone does not satisfy the code's standards.

Scenario B: A reporter is covering child marriage in a community with strong cultural norms around the practice. scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist reports on a child who has been reintegrated after time as a child soldier. Accurate reporting would use the phrase "former child soldier" — a precise factual description — but this label may permanently mark the child in their community and lead to rejection. The code prohibits its use if it causes such harm.
Scenario B: A story about HIV-affected families accurately identifies a child as HIV-positive using clinical language. That categorisation, even if factually precise, may expose the child to community discrimination. The code's mandatory identity-change rule and anti-stigmatisation rule both apply.
Scenario C: A journalist describes a child who has been exploited as a "child prostitute" — a term that is technically descriptive but widely understood to stigmatise and victim-blame. The code's prohibition on stigmatising categorisations applies regardless of whether the term is technically accurate.

Policy: Always change the name and obscure the visual identity of any child who is identified as: b. A perpetrator of physical or sexual abuse / d. Charged or convicted of a crime.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A 15-year-old is charged with a high-profile violent offence that has generated widespread public demand for information. policy_text: When in doubt about whether a child is at risk, report on the general situation for children rather than on an individual child, no matter how newsworthy the story.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: When in doubt about whether a child is at risk, report on the general situation for children rather than on an individual child, no matter how newsworthy the story.

Exceptions to this policy:
- The rule applies specifically "when in doubt" — it is a doubt-triggered default, not an absolute prohibition on individual reporting. Where risk can be clearly and affirmatively assessed as absent, the rule's operative condition is not met.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A journalist is unsure whether a child's account of trafficking can be published without endangering them, but the story is the most compelling individual narrative available. The code directs the journalist to report on child trafficking generally, not this child specifically.
Scenario B: A child in a conflict zone wants to give their account of displacement. The journalist cannot verify whether the child's family is safe or whether publication could endanger relatives still in the war zone. Doubt triggers the general-reporting default.
Scenario C: A child's story of surviving abuse would be transformative for a public awareness campaign about institutional failures. The journalist is uncertain whether publication would lead to retaliation against the child. The code's standard applies: uncertainty requires shifting to systemic rather than individual reporting.

policy_text: No staging: Do not ask children to tell a story or take an action that is not part of their own history.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: No staging: Do not ask children to tell a story or take an action that is not part of their own history.
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A documentary filmmaker asks a child to walk through the ruins of their former home for the camera to illustrate displacement, even though the child has not returned to that location voluntarily. The code prohibits this as staging — the action is being performed for the journalist's narrative, not as part of the child's own history.
Scenario B: A reporter asks a child to demonstrate a skill — such as making bricks — that they perform as part of their daily child-labour routine. This falls within "their own history" and is not prohibited staging; it is part of the child's authentic experience.
Scenario C: A journalist asks a child to describe an event they witnessed but did not directly experience (e.g., what happened to a sibling). This is ambiguous: the child can describe what they know, but cannot be asked to narrate or enact a story that is not their own.

editorial_dimension: presence of independent corroboration for a child witness's account
scenario_context: A local accident report in which a child is the witness to how a playground collapse occurred.
pole_a: Accept a child's account as credible testimony in its own right, as one would an adult's, and publish it without requiring independent corroboration — especially when the child is the primary witness.
pole_b: Confirm the accuracy of what a child says by seeking independent corroboration — preferably from both other children and an adult — before publishing.

policy_text: Confirm the accuracy of what the child has to say, either with other children or an adult, preferably with both.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Confirm the accuracy of what the child has to say, either with other children or an adult, preferably with both.

Exceptions to this policy:
- "Preferably with both" — the standard is aspirational at the highest level but accepts either a child or adult corroborant as a minimum
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A child describes witnessing an atrocity. The journalist cannot locate other witnesses but has no reason to doubt the child. The code requires seeking corroboration regardless of the journalist's personal assessment of the child's credibility.
Scenario B: A child's account of abuse at an institution is corroborated by other children who report similar experiences. The preferred standard is partially met; adding an adult corroborant (a social worker, teacher, or medical professional) would satisfy the full standard.
Scenario C: An adult source contradicts a child's account. The corroboration process has produced conflict rather than confirmation. The code does not specify how to resolve this — it stops at requiring the attempt to corroborate.

editorial_dimension: presence of independent corroboration for a child's eyewitness account of violence
scenario_context: A conflict-zone report in which a child recounts witnessing an attack on a village.
pole_a: Accept a child's account as credible testimony in its own right, as one would an adult's, and publish it without requiring independent corroboration — especially when the child is the primary witness.
pole_b: Confirm the accuracy of what a child says by seeking independent corroboration — preferably from both other children and an adult — before publishing.
text_pole_a: Soldiers set fire to the grain store before dawn and fired on families fleeing toward the river, a 10-year-old boy from the village recalled, pointing toward the charred building still smoldering behind him.
text_pole_b: Soldiers set fire to the grain store before dawn and fired on families fleeing toward the river, a 10-year-old boy from the village recalled, an account corroborated by two other children and a local aid worker who reached the scene that morning.
diff_span_pole_a: pointing toward the charred building still smoldering behind him
diff_span_pole_b: an account corroborated by two other children and a local aid worker who reached the scene that morning
policy_text: Confirm the accuracy of what the child has to say, either with other children or an adult, preferably with both.
policy_block:
The following policy from a journalistic code of ethics applies:

Policy: Confirm the accuracy of what the child has to say, either with other children or an adult, preferably with both.

Exceptions to this policy:
- "Preferably with both" — the standard is aspirational at the highest level but accepts either a child or adult corroborant as a minimum
scenarios_block:
Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario A: A child describes witnessing an atrocity. The journalist cannot locate other witnesses but has no reason to doubt the child. The code requires seeking corroboration regardless of the journalist's personal assessment of the child's credibility.
Scenario B: A child's account of abuse at an institution is corroborated by other children who report similar experiences. The preferred standard is partially met; adding an adult corroborant (a social worker, teacher, or medical professional) would satisfy the full standard.
Scenario C: An adult source contradicts a child's account. The corroboration process has produced conflict rather than confirmation. The code does not specify how to resolve this — it stops at requiring the attempt to corroborate.
